utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon all in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Wednesday 14th of January, 2009. Good afternoon to everyone, in particular to the accused, the Defence counsel, the OTP representatives, and all the people assisting us. Before the witness is brought in, the Trial Chamber is going to hand down an oral decision following the discussion we had yesterday following Mr. Kovacic's submissions and the request by Mr. Praljak to ask questions. I'm going to read slowly. Oral decision on the possibility for Mr. Kovacic to submit an application for review. At the hearing on the 13th of January, 2009, the accused Praljak through his counsel asked to cross-examine in person the expert witness on economic matters, Mr. Milan Cvikl. The Trial Chamber heard the submissions by Mr. Kovacic on this issue, and dismissed the application. After deliberation and after rereading the transcript, the Trial Chamber decides that there is no reason to grant the application by Mr. Kovacic to submit arguments for the Trial Chamber to review its decision denying accused Praljak the right to cross-examine in person the witness. The Trial Chamber, therefore, upholds its decision dismissing the issue handed down at the hearing of 13th of January, 2009 further to guide-line number 1 of the decision of the 24th of April, 2008. And further to the Appeals Chamber decision of 11th September, 2008, related to the appeal against the decision on examination of witnesses by Slobodan Praljak, a decision that had been issued by the Trial Chamber on the 26th of June, 2008. Therefore, Mr. Kovacic is not allowed to file an application for review. Therefore, Ms. Nozica, you will have 15 minutes for your questions to the witness as part of the cross-examination. Let's have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could make one remark while the witness is being brought in. As I've been preparing for the cross-examination, it's my colleague Mr. Kruger who was prepared to make any Prosecution submissions on the question of the matter that's just been decided by the Trial Chamber, so with the Court's permission could we ask that Mr. Kruger be allowed to leave the courtroom so that he can go back to work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, of course. I thought you wanted him to be able to speak, but of course he is allowed to leave the courtroom. I was happy to see him because I hadn't seen him in a long time, but of course he is free to leave the courtroom, I'm sure that he will be back in it soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Cvikl. Sorry for this slight delay of a few minutes, and Ms. Nozica is about to ask questions of you as part of the cross-examination. She may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Cvikl. I hoped that you have received my binder with the pink documents. If not I'll ask the usher to provide you with a copy. And let me say at the outset that you'll see out of the list of documents - and don't take fright because they're lengthy documents but I'm not going if go into them in detail, and you've already seen them - but here is the reason for my cross-examination. During yesterday's examination and if you look at page 81 of yesterday's transcript, I'd like to draw your attention to a question that Judge Antonetti asked you from line 18 onwards, on page 81 where Judge Antonetti noted that on the screen in front of you you had document 9551, and we can look at it now, page 42 of the English. And Judge Antonetti asked you, well he saw that there was a sum of 171 million which was the revenue of the minister of defence and he asked you whether of that 171 million was that used for the procurement of weapons and ammunition, and what about the worker's salaries, was that financed from the local budget as well. A question to that effect. Now, your answer is why I would like to cross-examine you today, because your answer was no. You say no. And that is 1993 you say and most of the costs, the ministry of defence from its revenues spent on financing units, and I think you say that the units which at that time were developed within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that those were the units and that the ministry did that taking care that the greatest part of those monies were spent on salaries, went to meet the salaries of the soldiers, expenses, and expenditure on weapons, but you said that you actually don't have any information about that. Do you remember that answer of yours? I assume you do.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we have the document before us, and it is P 9551, and we have the right page in front of us as well, and we see the sum within the budget, the budget revenue, page 42; right? Just a moment for me to check. Yes. Expenses, budget revenue and so on. Now, I'd like to ask you whether you conclude on the basis of the documents that you have seen that in 1993 they ceased to -- the municipalities ceased to finance defence or the local communes, whichever you like in, HZ HB. Is that what your answer means? That's how I understood. That's my interpretation of your answer, am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have said that I analysed the developments, economic developments in 1991, 1994 period by presenting three phases. Phase 1 in which the local communities were obviously the one which has the most of the power. And then period phase number 2 where already we have at the level of the region what we have seen for the 1992 a much more serious budget than let's say there was one in 1992 because in 1992 we have we see very small revenues as collected at the level of the region. And then in 1994 we have seen a much more developed interim -- a much more developed interim budget for the first half of 1994. At the same time, one could see that still in 1992 and 1993, there were still invalid [sic] some revenue collections measures at the level of local communities. So I cannot assume that in the 1993 the local communities stopped financing what I would assume were the logistics to the defence, but obviously the expenditure presented on this page, 43 of 83, certainly show that quite substantial amount of region-wide revenues collected at the level of the whole Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna went for the financing of the ministry of defence. What was exact activity at the level of local communities and what were exact budget expenditures at the level of local community, I cannot comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, in the transcript, witness, and I have understood you in that sense, on page 5, line 5, it is said there were still invalid some revenue measures. I think you wanted to say "in force" and not "invalid," that means void and non-existent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Still in force, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still in force, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, we have a clear-cut answer on your part which is the answer I understood it to be because from the document we can see how throughout 1993 the local budgets were -- well, the municipalities took part in the financing of defence. Now, Mr. Cvikl, I assume you don't challenge that this figure of 169 million, that these are sums expressed in Croatian dinars; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that this document has been prepared with total expenditures and there are a debate about it in some other pages like page 38 out of 83, that it talks about HR D, which are the Croatian dinars which were at that time one of the parallel currencies in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So I have assumed that there are some information in Deutschemark but that this lines are actually millions, actually hundreds of thousands of millions, which actually the billions of Croatian dinar at that time because in that very period the inflation was still extremely very high, so it must be in hundreds of millions of Croatian dinars.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you for that, but I would like to hurry you up by nodding my head because I have little time and a lot to get through. But just to be quite sure and to avoid any dilemmas in the courtroom, look at page 57 in English, and it is 00405251 ERN number in the Croatian version. And it is a report about social welfare and social benefits to families, and we see that expenditure there was 6215000 and in their financial report and page 57 in actual fact we see that and then on to the next page, page 58, and on page 58 paragraph 1 it says that for the previous year, including the 31st of December 1993, the Ministry of Labour Social Welfare and Family of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna has 6.045.000 Croatian dinars expenditures. So when we compare this financial report with the financial report of the ministry of finance, which is to be found on page 42, then we see that first of all we're dealing with Croatian Dinars, am I right there? And secondly there's slight discrepancy in the sum, it is 6 million [as interpreted] 045 in the one and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is 6 billion. 6 billion. Not 6 million.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Judge Trechsel, you are quite right. That's what I wanted to say. It isn't 169 or 170 million, it is in fact -- well for the ministry of defence, but billions in Croatian dinars of course. So we see that we are dealing with Croatian dinars, that's the first point. And the second point that's important for me was what we just established. So within the frameworks of this report from the ministry for social welfare and family affairs, they say that they spent -- that their expenditures were 6 billion 045 million, and in the expenditures and the report by the ministry of finance the figure is slightly higher.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cvikl, as an economist yourself, I'm sure you can explain that and it's clear to everyone that they don't have to be the same sums, the sums don't have to coincide exactly because each ministry has its own financial plan and keeps its records but the ministry of finance has exact data as to expenditures from the revenues coming in from the HVO, HZ HB am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that a small difference on page 58 compared to the one on page 43, which is something like 150 million must be some of the -- what we call in budgetary expenditure appropriation, that may be wages of the employees of the ministry where they are really explaining what this money on the page 58 had been spent for. And the most important is, of course, that here they are indicating that they were spending money to provide aid to socially deprived persons and, of course, they transferred the most of this 6 billion dollars the amount of 5.1 billion dollars they transferred to pension insurance, pension disability insurance, which means that ministry of labour has -- has to finance the pension disability insurance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, in this document, the one that we have in front of us, and you've already commented on that, it is the report of the HVO HZ HB, at the beginning and later on, the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna there is no financial report of the defence department. You didn't find it, right? There is no separate financial report of the defence department. We have the department of defence first, parts of it, and at the end there is no financial report, am I right there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a general description of what the minister of defence was doing but no details.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in your answer, in your response to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a follow-up question, Mr. Cvikl. Yesterday we saw documents showing at least that a budget had been established. As to whether this was an interim or an operational budget, I don't have an answer based on examining the documents, but if we assume that this was a budget with items for various activities, ministry of defence, social ministry, ministry for education, so we have certain amounts earmarked by ministry. And Ms. Nozica is telling us that with regard to the defence department, there were no documents showing how the budget was implemented, but you know this budgetary system. Therefore, can you tell us whether you found any indication showing that within the main budgetary items there could be credit transfers, that a certain amount would have been given to a ministry initially but then for some reason it was decided to use part of that money in another ministry? Is that something that could be done at the time, was it possible to have credit transfer in spite of the initial budget allocations to various ministries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the information which we have in front of us is the information on actual expenditures. We don't here see what would be a usual normal presentation of the budget where there would be initial allocation, changes in a year, and then the final outcomes and final outlays as when the year is over. So I can't comment what were the changes between the initial allocation and actual final utilisation of the allocated funds. We can't see that from the pages in front of us. We just see the final end of year account of the budget.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm satisfied with your answer. If there is a budget of course, there are expenditures, that's what you've just said, and income. And normally a budget should be balanced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, I see, and I'm very surprised to see that, please look at page 62 of the latest document. Page 62. You know it's always dangerous when you present a document because if you have a judge who is inquisitive he might find grounds for asking questions. Page 62, what do I see, there are donors and they are mentioned by name, UNICEF, ADRA, ERC, Red Cross, et cetera, Caritas. That's page 62, so I suppose these donors donated funds which should be registered as income, shouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it depends. If the funds are in cash, then usually that would be legally and included in the budget. But here I see that these were 2.160 tonnes of the quantity of received aid, and I don't know whether and page 42 out of 83, under item 4, donation and other revenues the figure which is there 57 -- 57 billion dinars is the value of these funds calculated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. But let's assume that Caritas donated a given amount of money which would be regarded as income or revenue and with a budgetary system that a Caritas money could have been used to buy -- to purchase weapons because you don't itemize the budget expenditures Caritas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, usually the donors -- I mean, that would be the normal system, also request what the money should be spent for, and usually there's an obligation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the donation and a donor where the recipient to the donation should prove what money was spent for. So I don't believe that the Caritas, if there was cash a transaction would be allowing buying of weaponry. But I don't have, you know, information what was the actual cash, cash monies received from Caritas and what it was spent in what kind. I would assume given the information on page 62 that most of it was aid, which means really providing funds needed for the survival of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Agreed, but in case the donations would have been cash donations through swift transfer or in cash, nothing in budget terms prevents that money to be used otherwise, because there's no itemisation of the expenditures. It's just a theoretical hypothesis that I'm expressing here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on hypothetical questions I have very difficult to answer, but if one does follow good public expenditures management practice, that would not be possible because as I have said, a donor would usually request and define the purpose of a particular donation. So even, you know, once in 1995, 1996 the World Bank was start giving loans, it was very clear we would give loan for either financing of the repair of the courthouse or as a what we call a general government or budget support. But donors like the one mentioned on page 62, UNICEF, et cetera, they would usually have actual material goods that they would provide to the population, and usually the contribution by the local communities or the Croatian community would be providing the logistical support of transfer of those things. But as I say, I cannot comment whether cash from Caritas was eventually used for the buying of weaponry. I would -- I would -- I don't assume that, but I can't you know, of course clearly answer to your question because I don't have information on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But just to correct what we've just been discussing, I have been asking you questions and so has His Honour Judge Antonetti about the expenditures, the spending of the funds that the minister of defence had, and then His Honour Judge Antonetti showed you page 62. But I would like us to look at page 60 of this document. Let us look at whose expenditures or revenues we are talking about. This is the sector for social welfare and family. And the donations that are discussed here are under the heading of the service for the gathering and distribution of humanitarian aid. Mr. Cvikl, it's not controversial that this sector and this service could not have been a part of the department of defence. I don't have enough time to go through the whole structure but it does appear to be quite logical to me. It is a completely different sector which is part of a completely different ministry that is now showing the funds that it received. Could you please confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you to look at page 60. That's in the English version. We are talking about the humanitarian aid that His Honour Judge Antonetti was talking about. We can see here on page 60 and forward to page 62 that it all relates to report of the centre for social welfare and family, and the humanitarian aid listed at page 62 is part of the report that is filed by the service for the collection and distribution of humanitarian aid. Now, my question to you is these funds were collected within another ministry, not the ministry of defence am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We not here discuss the ministry of defence expenditure. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you, we do have a document, it's a report -- it's a financial report of the defence department and the ministry of defence because this is for the whole of 1993. That's P 8118. I can see that you found it. And in this document, let me remind the Chamber, that as regards the revenues of the department in 1993 and the expenditures through all the items in the budget were discussed with witness Miroslav Rupcic who testified before this Tribunal between the 7th of October, 2007 and the 10th of October, 2007. Unfortunately I don't have enough time to go through the whole document, but I would like to ask you this: The first question, in drafting your report did you consult this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen all details of that document, and I believe that this document with all these details, I see it now more or less for the first time because I was not able, you know, to have it. I mean, I don't recall this document. And it seems to be a very detailed financial expenditures what would usually be done at the level of the ministries where the other report which I was citing is the overall report of the whole HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That's correct. If we are talking about the financing of the municipalities, and I would like to pursue this topic, please look at page 4 in the English version of this report. I think that page 7 has been marked for your convenience, but could you please just leaf backwards to page 4. We see the introductory remarks here and then we see the fifth passage here where it says in the previous period, the system of logistic support or MFP was established within the following restricting circumstances. Have you found it? All I'm interested in is item 2. You can see that it is listed under number 2, the self-financing of the HVO units through municipal bodies. So in this financial report, it is indicated that throughout 1993, the financing continued. Let me now refer you to page 7 briefly, that is the structure of the revenues, we don't have time to go through all of it, and we can see that in the structure of the revenues, the total was 148 billion, out of that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's remark: Could the counsel please repeat the figures that she was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can see that the total was 204 billion and the total revenue was 185 billion. We saw in the document of the financing for the HVO for 1993 that the revenues totalled 170 billion. And Mr. Cvikl, since you don't have enough time to deal with all this, is it possible, could you please tell us whether it is possible at all according to you as an expert in economics that the revenues that individual ministries are showing can differ from the revenues shown by the ministry of finance because probably in the circumstances the records were kept in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is clearly possible. As I have said, and I think that your additional information provide, confirm what I was saying about the types of expenditures that were done at the level of the minister of defence, and that is on page 10 where it's obvious that are payment of gross calculated revenues and compensations for the soldiers, and then other material expenses and services linked with the minister of defence. It is possible clearly as we have seen also in previously ministry of work and social services that there are differences between what would be a financial information on financial support from 1st of January to 31st of December, 1993, that difference could be for two reasons. One, the budget expenditures and the budget revenues are usually provided on cash basis, while for a particular ministry, this may be even important what they were getting in kind or what they were getting as a credit so there could be a difference between the two figures. But for what I believe is the most important, that the region-wide expenditures that were collected provided for not just the ministry of the defence but all other ministries, funds need so they have undertaken region-wide social and state measures as they would have been -- as they should have been provided by the central authorities but they have not. And in that context, my analysis goes that the fact that we have a serious budget revenues and budget expenditures presented for the 1993 at the level of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is that they have undertaken measures that would be otherwise need to be undertaken by the central government authority which of course hadn't happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I fully agree, I did not go into that part of the examination because I do believe that you did explain this quite well, but let me now go back to a number of documents and then I will be asking you my questions. But these are documents that should show whether the local authorities and to what extent in 1993 financed the defence of the HVO HZ HB. It's a small binder. Let us forget about the big documents and let us now move through it quickly. These are all the documents that you saw in the course of your proofing, I assume, if not, please tell us so. I will go through all those documents very quickly. The first is 1D 310. It's a decision on the financing of the HVO Livno and of the sanctioning of persons subject to military obligation. The decision dated the 26th of March, 1993. The next document is 1D 00307. It's a decision allocating financial aid to the Bruno Busic HVO regiment, and it was issued by the municipal HVO of Livno. The date is the 24th of April, 1993. So those documents are sequential. There's one document for each month or maybe two months. The next document is 1D 00302. The date is the 13th of May, 1993. Again it is a decision of the Livno municipal HVO about financing of the defence of the Livno municipality HVO by farmers and cattle breeders. The next document is 1D 00299. Again, it is the Livno municipal HVO. This is a decision to grant financial assistance, compensation to members of the Luka Josic 2nd Military Police Light Assault Battalion who had arrived from Bugojno. Just two more documents and we'll be done. The next document is 1D 00295. It's a decision about the setting of salaries for the village commanders, again it's the Livno municipal HVO. The date is the 23rd of November 1993. And finally, Mr. Cvikl, I think that this is really the most important document enabling us to determine who financed whom in 1993. That's document 1D 3036. Let me just briefly tell you that this is a document signed by the head of the HVO of the Tomislavgrad municipality. The date is the 15th of January, 1994. The memo was sent to the Ministry of Finance to the attention of the minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It deals with the import of cigarettes, and in the first paragraph the drafter explains why he actually sends this memo to the minister. I will be reading this and please follow. "In our previous response to your serious accusations again Mr. Philip Andric, we stated that we support work order, legality, and a unified system both in financial terms and in any other way in the area of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, but due to the sloppiness of the public administration it is not possible to draw the line between financial and every other chaos on the one hand, and the order and legality in the financial area and in other areas on the other hand. And this is now the key issue. This line according to you, according to the minister should commence with the date of the session of the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna parliament. However, we are of the opinion that it was your responsibility to inform all the municipal HVOs through an appropriate document about the exact date when the different method of financing of the needs of the army was to commence, and to also inform all the military units so that they would not approach by force of habit the municipal HVOs for the funds they need to meet their needs, but would rather contact operational zones of the Main Staff of the HVO. It would also have been necessary to anticipate what to do if the logistics of the operational zone and of the Main Staff were not able to meet even the most basic needs of the military units as has been the case in most cases. Since as of December the 8th of 1993 such a document had not been distributed." This is sufficient for my question. So my question is this,

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIKL
utterances.text: First of all, have you had an opportunity to look at those documents and to read them.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw these documents in preparation as I have said, still in 1993 while there was on one side a budget had been established. At the level of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, there was continuation of activity because there were either new matters or old matter still valid. I could not say at what points in time was a line set.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you whether you have had an opportunity to look at the previous documents, the previous four or five decisions from the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... specially this assistant to the Bruno Busic and to contributions for the Livno people are not reporting. I've seen those documents, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, I know that you quote them in your report, but I for the purpose of this specific question to put them to you. Finally, Mr. Cvikl, from the last document signed by the president of the Tomislavgrad HVO, does it not follow that not only throughout 1993 but also into 1994, the defence was for the most part financed from the municipal budgets, because here it is stated quite clearly when we talk to the Main Staff they are unable to meet our demands and this is how it has been for the most part. So on the basis of all those documents and I do not want to discount the efforts that you took to explain that the Croatian government of -- the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and before that the executive body of the HZ HB, did they put in an effort to pool all the resources in one place and then distribute, that this did not happen throughout 1993. Could you please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that there were major disputes between local communities and of course Croatian Defence Council mainly for two reasons. In 1992 you have a situation where local communities have established their own economy and those that were better off did not want to give up their quote revenues. But -- and that's why it was very difficult for the Croatian Defence Council as a temporary executive authority to undertake those measures. I also understood that there were dispute, you know, why you are reactivating Social Accounting Office if Social Accounting Office is taking money from us. But that does not mean that it was not appropriate that HVO, Croatian Defence Council, has been undertaking those measures because that was the only way how down the line you would have only one region-wide budget because it would be illogical to have, quote, 18 ministers of defence or 20 ministers of defence on the local communities. On the other side, according to the existing, you know, central government legislation, especially the one on the covering the social needs, financing of the defence was a top level priority. For all of the -- for all the communities being local communities or region-wide communities. So this letter which you are presenting here is very similar to many letters that are between the ministries and local communities even to today in Slovenia when there is a dispute, you know, who financed what, when. And so I would, I cannot say that because this is the belief of the head of the option of Tomislavgrad that in the 1993, the majority of the funds were financed from the local communities. One would have to do a very deep analysis, what was the overall expenditures, what were the actual expenditures, what were those expenditures that were authorised, because one has to be careful on, you know, what were the activities that were financed and that were actually undertaken by the defence units. Were those all as instructed by the Main Staff. So you know, one cannot say on the basis of just one letter, and there is obviously a dispute between the ministry of finance and the local communities that, you know, for these very reason local communities were the only one financing the defence needs. But they were of course contributing what they could. And frankly speaking, if they were not, if they were not as one could also see sending to the region-wide budget all the funds collected, they should be doing this. They should be financing the defence as the first priority because that has been said by many document and that was obviously the most important need.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, you were not asked whether the municipalities for the most part, I only asked whether they participated in the financing, not whether they did it for the most part, but as regards let me just ask you a very brief question. As regards what you just told us that we should look at the revenues and expenditures, we do have a report from the defence department where both expenditures and revenues are shown. And I have a hypothetical question for you, that's going to be my last question, I allow myself the right to ask you that because in the course of yesterday you were asked this. Well, on the basis of your experience in Slovenia, can you assume that the municipalities did have this opinion about the financing throughout this time because self-financing afforded them a possibility to have political and any other influence over the units that they were financing? Can you confirm that this segment was quite significant and relevant on the basis of your experience, if you can, if you cannot, well you were asked something about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... I would like to really understand what are you asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether the efforts of the municipalities to directly finance the defence in their own areas, the units that are located in their areas, whether their effort to do that as we can see throughout 1993 as well, whether this followed from their wish to control the units that they were financing, political control over those units over the defence of their area, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with this view. I think that the main reason why local municipalities would object to finance, to put all the revenues collected on their own territories they sent to the region-wide budget is mainly dealt with the fear that on the apportionment through the budget they would not be receiving back what they believe they should. And that's always -- in the budget preparation there's always dispute between the one who is "collecting" or used to collect very important funds at the - let's say - custom checkpoint and he -- and they believe that they still shall be receiving so much funds. I can give you many examples in this public expenditure management where there are disputes about this, but I would not assume that they wanted to finance the defence unit in order to politically control them. I mean, I have not been looking into that, but from my public expenditures management experience the disputes between the higher level and the lower level of the government is also this difference of opinion what is the particular budget should really give to a particular either smaller unit being -- ministry or local municipality. We see in the budgetary debate a lot of discussion on this and that's why it's always very good if the budget adopted by parliament, by the house of representatives. And the once the House of Representatives adopted it, it's obligable for everyone, or in that very case it was adopted I believe by the HVO which was appointed by the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna of course consisted of many -- of all representatives of local municipalities and that's -- that's -- that was, you know, a kind of a political fight at the level of presidency what should be financed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Finally, to conclude, Mr. Cvikl, you say -- you answered to my question that this could not have been the intention, could it have been a consequence, because now you say that you don't know what size the units were at the local level. I don't want to go into that. I think that we have evidence to that effect. I'm asking you whether this could have been a consequence of precisely this fact, that the local level, regardless of the size of the units, was actually financing it. Let us assume, hypothetically, for the most part in 1993 it financed the units in its local area. Could have it have been a consequence of the possibility of exerting some other kind of control political military?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of economic measures and activities within the overall economic environment. I had not looked into what was happening in the area of defence finance. I mean, I was in Yugoslav Army but I was not asked to look into it, so I can't comment on that. But again, the analysis of the economic measures from the economic point of view where there were appropriate measures to undertake at the level of the region expenditures that would not be undertaken by the local communities themselves. And that is the -- that is what am I seeing in this phase 2 and phase 3. We could have three years just phase 1 if they would not be activities at the region-wide measures and then, you know, kids would not go to school and the roads would not be repaired, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much, Mr. Cvikl, you finally gave us your answer, you did not conduct this kind of analysis and I take your previous answer in that light. So you did not make an analysis of the effect that it had on the financing of the army and you did not have any documents that would lead you to be able to give an answer to that question. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... economic issues. And I looked into the budgetary expenditures for the defence in the point of the budget of a wide region.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Cvikl, this completes my cross-examination. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, we will now begin the cross-examination by the Prosecution. That must be ready because it has been waiting for this for several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President, and good afternoon to you and to Your Honours and to everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Cvikl. My name is Douglas Stringer. I'll be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution, and we've got binders to distribute and we've got documents to show you. While that's being done, just let me ask you to go back to the pink folder that you were shown by counsel for Mr. Stojic. I'll just ask you one question there before I get into my own outline. If you could turn to the Exhibit P 09551, page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak is standing up. Yes, Mr. Praljak, what do you wish to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had hoped that you would change your opinion and that is why I didn't discuss the matter with Mr. Kovacic, but as you didn't reconsider well I don't want to go into that now, but anyway, before we take a break, may I ask through -- ask Mr. Kovacic to ask the witness two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you'd like your counsel to put two questions. Well, in that case, there's no problem. Mr. Kovacic, there are two questions. You have the floor. In the meantime, we will assemble the bulky folders of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may request a short break of 5 minutes to see exactly what because yesterday Mr. Praljak mentioned but now he summarized --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, very well. The best thing would be for us to have the break now that we planned to have a little later on. So for 5 minutes you can talk to Mr. Praljak which will allow you to put the two questions and the Registrar will have given us all the -- overburdened us with all the binders, kilos and kilos, and we the Judges will have 20 minutes to prepare for the next part. So we now have the 20 minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, just a brief observation. During the break I was approached, I won't say by whom, but I was approached just to caution everybody that it would be wonderful if the witness could slow down a little bit, enunciate more, and if there could be a pause between question and answer, it would be facilitate everybody. And so I would most appreciate it, and again, I apologise for having to make this observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, point taken. So please do try to slow down, Witness. Well, I'm telling this to the counsel as well who are faster than lightening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness. My name is Bozidar Kovacic and I'm Defence counsel for General Praljak, one of the accused in this case, and I'm going to ask you a few questions to see if we can expand some of your observations. Your Honours -- Their Honours and you have received 3D 02653, that particular document, you have the English version and you have the Croatian version. So you can choose. I think that the Croatian version is more legible but it's up to you. If you choose the Croatian, then it will be page 152 and 153. For the rest looking at the English, it is page 1 of the English translation, and I'm going to start off by asking something around line 30, with a sentence that begins: "The truth was that the assembly of the SMBH..." et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kovacic, I think it would be quite helpful if you told the Chamber what this is, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- put your attention to the appropriate portion, then I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in e-court. It is an excerpt, or rather several pages from a book by Mohammed Filipovic, and the book is entitled, "I was Alija's Diplomat." And the author of the book, Mr. Filipovic, was ambassador of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to Switzerland in 1992 and 1993. So during the relevant period, the material time. Now, witness, the highlighted portion states the following, let's go straight to the crux of the matter, and then we'll go back to discuss other points perhaps. This is what he says, as I say, it's around line 13 in English. "The truth was that the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina following a proposal from the government adopted a law making it the responsibility of all our citizens working abroad to pay a certain percentage (5 percent) of their net income as a so-called war tax for financing the war and post-war reconstruction of the country." Let's pause there. My question is the following: You found examples during your testimony about this war tax, and I think you used the example of two or three municipalities. Did you ever hear that the same step was taken by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, because here we learn, although we don't have that decision, that the government too wanted to impose a special tax on migrant workers of this type. And then we see that this referred to the people who happened to be working in Switzerland. Did you happen to hear about that, if not see a document as well to bear it out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw documents on local municipality imposing a war tax on people that were mobilised. And in order for them not to be mobilised, not to report to the duty station, they could instead of that pay 200, 300 Deutschemark of a monthly contribution which I found as in a kind of exemption from them being mobilised. On this very event which you are mentioning here, that they also -- the Assembly of the Bosnia-Herzegovina upon proposal of the government, I have not seen such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Have you heard anything about that that Sarajevo government also tried to enact some taxes related to the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we were discussing with authorities in 1994, 1995 we were aware there were different attempts to, you know, collect, but I have not in my analysis being analysing in details what the central government authorities were doing in 1993, 1994. I was focusing on the developments of the level of the local municipalities and region-wide measures, and I looked into the overall budget of the 1992 Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina where I could see that there were no support provided down to the local municipalities. So I found it completely logical that they went ahead with the measures given the fact that they were authorised to do that by a decree law on the financing of social needs as issued in the summer of 1992 by then the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] While you were there as you say in 1994, 1995, in that IMF mission, did you happen to come across any traces of any money coming in as revenue to the state from some -- well, let's call it war tax regardless of what it was actually called since you had the basic information?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this question we would object. It's beyond the scope of the expert report. Again, the witness is here based on what is in his expert report, and I don't think it's fair to the Prosecution to now go into information and in a detailed way that he may have gathered 1994, 1995 which is not really the subject of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't agree with that position. In fact the witness was talking about being there as a member of IMF and having some knowledge about the situation also from that opportunity. And now I'm merely asking whether while doing that he saw or learned about any result of this which we were talking. Any result in the budget of taxation of migrant workers taxation. It's a simple question, it's yes or no and it is certainly within the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer, I believe that it is difficult to understand your objection because the expert is an economist, he has looked into budgets, into the budget of Herceg-Bosna with revenues and expenditures. So the question was, looking at all the documents, whether as part of the World Bank or the IMF, whether he realised whether there were revenues arising from contributions made by people working abroad. As was indicated -- as seems to be indicated for the Muslim side this document. It seems to be logical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand and I certainly accept the Trial Chamber's ruling. I think the point I'm trying to make, Your Honour, is that Mr. Cvikl in his report has very specifically laid out what were the scope of the items. He relied on -- relied upon the documents provided by counsel, he relied upon the interviews of the people he spoke with, he -- and so the scope of the universe of things that he has relied on to support his opinions are set out there. And I could be wrong, but I don't think that he has relied to any significant degree on information he obtained by having dealings with people in Warsaw in 1994, 1995. Certainly he has not indicated that that forms a part of his opinions as indicated in his report. But I won't make any more objections on this, Mr. President, it's clearly the Trial Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I do not agree with that argument, but you have decided and there is no need to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From this the following question emerges, the legality of taxes of that type. And in this specific case, in this case, judging by this piece of information, the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has set a tax as an obligation, let's call it the war tax, it impose this is tax on its citizens who are legal residents in Switzerland in this case, and come under those laws, the laws of the country, and now you as a financial expert probably have knowledge in this area too, tell us whether it is permissible for a government to impose taxes on citizens living in another country?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it all depends what is the tax, where this particular citizen have a tax residence. But as I've said, when I was looking into the local municipality decisions and whether the decision by the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was of a similar nature, these people that were supposed to pay taxes were people with a permanent residence on the territory of the local municipalities. And as we the permanent residence, they were obliged to report on the mobilisation. However, some of the local municipalities decided not to or excused them from reporting on the mobilisation, and they were saying that they could not report on their duty for mobilisation if they are paying a special -- a contribution special tax. So in that very case I say that possible. In general whether Bosnia-Herzegovina would be able to tax citizens that are gastarbeiters, gas workers in Switzerland, and to what extent, that depends on two issues. Where particular citizens have a tax residence and what is an agreement between the two countries or what was agreement at that time between the two, I guess Switzerland in that very case and at that time I guess Yugoslavia or Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, I would like to also say that the recent economic development report of the IMF, which I'm citing in the report, on page 100 it explains that there are some so-called non-tax revenues in Bosniak majority area in 1994 and 1995 and that could be enough, that this could be, you know, items that you put in the budget as a non-tax revenue if it's coming from abroad. But this is, you know, one would have to do a much deeper analysis and we were not - neither the World Bank, neither IMF - at that time concerned what happened in the past, we were looking how to make the system for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in actual fact from the writings of Mr. Filipovic in this book of his, we see a little lower down, and I mark that too. We see two things firstly, that the Swiss government launched a protest and sent a demarche to the embassy saying that this was impermissible; and secondly, as we can see from this text, the author says the following: The truth was that the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina following a proposal from the government adopted a law et cetera, et cetera, we've already read that bit out. And then it goes on to say that at a meeting of all our ambassadors and diplomatic consular representatives abroad held in early 1994 in Vienna, some of us attempted to point out that our state did not have the right to make it the responsibility of people working in foreign countries and subject to the laws of those countries, i.e., under their full jurisdiction, to pay a tax to our country. It was particularly impossible to ask these citizens to pay a tax on their net income. And to cut this story short, that this wasn't discussed and it was refused. So there were different opinions set out, but briefly, it seem that is you agree that it was possible that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina did try to impose this tax, whether it did or did not ultimately, you find traces of that or possible traces of that in the budget; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the reading of what you have read to us, there seems to be obviously such an attempt, but whether it was legally correct or not, it's for me difficult to judge. If the gastarbeiters in Switzerland were also tax residents of Switzerland it was not correct and it was correct that these this fellow, Mr. Filipovic, objected to that at that meeting. And I also read that later on he changed his obligation into kind of a voluntary contribution. I have not been looking into this 1994 what was happening in this various situation. When I was looking into there what local municipalities were doing, would like to point again, people were to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Witness, we don't have the time, we understand that and instead they were paying taxes. But here we saw that similar attempt was done by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo-based government; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] It's not in 3D that's just the source. Anyway an introductory question first. Witness, I'm sure you know Stijepo Andrejevic, a doctor of science, the governor -- Andric I'm told, yes, Andric is his name -- Andrijic, that's what it says here, Andrijic. Stijepo Andrijic. He was the governor of the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina and as far as I know highly reputable economist. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have an excerpt here from his book, the book is by Stijepo Andrijic. He deals with several topics and I'm just going to read two observations of his. Let me lay the foundations first. You said that certain municipalities, not only in the area of HZ HB but elsewhere too, prescribed -- well, the German Mark, introduced the German Mark or the Croatian dinar as legal tender, as the currency, in order to effect payments through the SDK or social accounting service, or the system that substituted the former SDK. Similar information exists here so I'd like to hear your comments. The first thing that he says --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry for the interruption. Am I missing something. I don't -- do I have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't. It's just for my purpose I will read.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You are just going to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I will not ask that -- it to be admitted as the evidence, I simply read it as well I can read my notes, whatever, and the witness does not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The author says as follows --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they do not have the text either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: "It is important to emphasize the fact that in Tuzla and Zenica, those areas at the end of 1992 already, the political and military portions, which means the state bodies, reached a decision on the use of the German Mark as the legal tender of the country. And there were separate coupons printed in German Marks, you also testified about that, for the requirements of the payment system. And this brings me to the portion we are interested in. This fact -- there was no official reaction to this fact from the state organs in Sarajevo. In the autumn of 1993 he goes on to say - and that was after I was replaced as governor - the new government in Sarajevo passed a regulation by which it introduced the German Mark as legal tender. As the official currency of the country. "And on the basis of that regulation and the institutions dealing with payments, all legal persons were duty-bound to open giro accounts in German Marks and they had to effect payments in that way. Those accounts were in use and the German Mark became legal tender right up until the formation of the central bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the introduction of a new currency, that is to say the convertible Mark." So the governor of the national bank of Croatia in his book -- I meant to say Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was a slip of the tongue, he writes in this official book of his, that the government in Sarajevo proclaimed the German Mark legal tender. And in your expert report and working on your expert report you found proof that this was done in other municipalities as well and you explained the importance of that step. Now, have you ever heard of the fact that this was done in Sarajevo and if not, do you agree with what the governor -- the then-governor of the national bank says?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do agree with what the former governor of the national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina says because this was a situation which I already have said yesterday, 1992, 1993 there were extremely high, hundreds of thousands percentage high inflation and even if the Bosnian dinars were printing usually in such circumstance, you know, the printing machines do not work fast enough. And so it's logical that not Deutschemark as the only legal tender but Deutschemark as a para-legal tender could have been introduced. And I was mostly interested, that was my task, to look was happening at the level of local communities and I found that they are quite logical. And I'm not surprised that that happened up to the point that convertible mark had been established also at the level of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And all that remains is one thing, that he also states here: Shortly after the domestic currency was introduced, it was devalued. You spoke about that, too. So I don't want to read his entire explanation as to why that happened, but he does point out one more thing and that is that the national bank at the same time did not have the possibility of printing additional paper money for three reasons; technical feasibilities or lack of them, it did not have any foreign exchange for paying for the printing of a new currency, and third, the costs of printing would exceed the nominal value of the coupons. It took longer to print the money, the money devalued faster than it took to print the money. So under this hyperinflation which is contained in these assertions, was it possible at all to issue proper money?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proper money would be possible to be issued only if the fiscal revenues collected at the level of the whole country would be sufficient enough to finance expenditures which was not the case. And I have mentioned in comparing what was happening in at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina what was happening at the level of Croatian Community of the Herceg-Bosna and what we have seen in comparing the inflation rates in different parts, that obviously the republican issued money was more prone to devaluation and that's why it's logical that sometimes 1992, 1993 they simply actually were not able to print it enough, and that's why the Deutschemark became a para-legal tender. It's just a logical reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I may summarise in a question, for the same reasons, objective reasons, where the citizens used the money that it had in order to exchange money for goods, would that be right? Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the para-legal tenders to buy and sell goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. [In English] Just one question by the way. [Interpretation] During your testimony, among other things, you used the International Monetary Fund report dated August 1996, 1D 02959. So just a short question about that. After the IMF compiled that report in the summer of 1996, was it accessible to public institutions? For example, the United Nations, the European Union, and other interested organs and parties? Or let me be more specific, for example, the Prosecution of this Tribunal, could it ask the IMF about the monetary and economic situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for instance, what the IMF knows about that, and would the IMF respond and provide them with that information? You were there, you worked within the system. What would you say to that, what is what's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the document, the recent economic development report which was issued and became publicly available at least to the, you know, UN related institutions and International Monetary Fund is a UN-related institution should -- be could be made available to anyone requesting it. There were also joint press releases ordered in the November of 1995 for this economic situation was described, so I would be looking to this documents before making any opinion. And that's why I have said. For me the IMF report and the World Bank reports, these two reports were also the, you know, basis. I have of course contributed to Croatian, at least the World Bank report were also the basis of kind of getting the big picture and then looking into details. I did on the basis of looking at the document which I collected through the help of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But just looking at those two reports, by a third party, somebody who has a general level of educational knowledge, that would be enough for them to learn a great deal about the economic and monetary problems of the situation in general in Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1992, 1993, 1994 would that be correct? Just yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, sir. [Interpretation] Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And good afternoon again, Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's start if we may. I just wanted to preliminarily take you to one of the exhibits that my learned friends Ms. Nozica showed you. It's in the pink folder, Exhibit P 09551. If you could turn to page 62 of the English. This actually was in relation to a question from the president with regard to any funds or aid coming from humanitarian organisations. The President asked you whether to what extent based on your knowledge it may have been possible to actually trace where any funding from such organisations actually ultimately went. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just looking -- I went ahead and looked at the next paragraph, and there were references to tonnes of humanitarian aid here. Would you agree with me, sir, that for example, according to this report, which is sort of a year-end report of the various activities of the HVO, of the various departments of the HVO. This indicates that of 2.160 tonnes of humanitarian aid that had been obtained or received from these organisations, 520 tonnes appears to have been distributed to HVO units. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then secondly an additional 240 tonnes of aid had been distributed to government institutions and organs, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think I know the answer clearly, but just for the record, you didn't consider in any of your analyses, the extent to which goods in kind figured as part of the budget or of the resources of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We have not seen a detailed -- we have seen some nominal figures. How these figures were calculated, whether these were estimates of the funds collected, how was that then distributed, I did not venture into that analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You can set that aside, I've finished with that document now. Just a couple of preliminary questions about your report, Mr. Cvikl. Can you tell us when you were first contacted by the Prlic Defence team to begin working on this project, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The report was finalized in October of 2008; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then working backwards, you made the field trip to Bosnia-Herzegovina in December of 2007 where you conducted the interviews?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly from your report, the field trip and the interviews occurred after you had reviewed the various documentation that you refer to in your report; is that correct in general?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I first collect the information. I add to this information which I had received from the Defence team, you know, I trace back the IMF report, I trace back the World Bank report which I have in my own files since I was working on it. I looked into the -- you know, again these 2004 World Bank book on the collapse of Yugoslavia, I read over some other documents. And then when I was reading that I actually identify a need to, you know, to visit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sure?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- again Bosnia-Herzegovina in this very -- in this very connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Before your field trip and before the interviews, did you also review the documents provided by Mr. Karnavas, the Defence team, the various decrees, the Official Gazette, those sorts of basic documents as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I went on a field trip but didn't really do interviews but I was kind of discussing with the people the content of those documents, yes. So I had these documents, some of them with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So the field trip was in December of 2007. Then working backward from that, can you give us a rough idea of when you actually began working then on this project?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that I was a member of parliament, so most of my work and kind of, you know, reading the documents was in the late summer, fall of 2007. And then just before actually preparing for that field trip, I was kind of, you know, collect the document and from the document also identify okay, which of the people that I would like to see. I at that time had suggested to go to Zagreb to see some people there, to go to Tuzla, to go to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We'll actually talk more about the interviews in a little bit. Sort of focusing on the documents and also the time-frame or the chronology. As you've indicated you were a member of parliament, the Slovenian parliament at the time that you were working on this report; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I was at that time 2004, 2008, I was a member of parliament and I have worked on that report and some other books under the authority which is given to a politician, and he can do what we call an expert work or work as a, you know, professor university up to one-fifth of his time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you expect that the report that you've made for this case will ultimately be published and be available more widely than it already is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not -- that's not yet decided. I mean, this is up to the -- you know, I have prepared the report for this very case. It is certainly I believe a document which provides a kind of a wide picture on what was actually happening. Would there be -- would there be at one point in time a need, I don't know. But certainly, I would not be -- I have not prepared this report to have a book on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Have you been compensated for your preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I was paid from the ICTY for this, whatever the amount was, something like you know 150 hours by the hourly rate. But I must say I spent more than 150 hours on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you write the report entirely on your own?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The report has been written by myself. I got assistance from the Defence team in this finalization of the report, you know, the language, the -- you know, some editing, and then also they were helping me in organising the report, especially the foot notes and, you know, how properly putting this, you know, special numbers, you know, 1D numbers and P numbers because I didn't understand the at beginning how that correctly should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Many of us still don't.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that D is for Defence and P is for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So members of the Prlic Defence team then assisted you in doing some editing and revising of the report, is that what I understand you to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more less, I would say editing it, editing. Because I prepared the report in the, you know, early in the early version with all the table of contents, et cetera. Initially there were literature at the end, then we made some of these changes and, you know, put the things. They helped me put in this finalization of the report, yes. But I -- the report has been written by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss any of the text of the report with them in a substantive way as part of that revision or editing process?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. Not really. Because I had been asked, you know, by this letter of appointment, and so I decided myself how to structure it and how much emphasis to put on that, on the background and how much to put on the events. And my kind of -- I was sort of doing this from the point of that will be read by of course people who are not looking into these documents but who do not have a wider knowledge. And of course, as I've said yesterday, I especially wanted honours, the Judges of the court to have appreciation of the developments, the way I presented them because they are based on the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you confer with Dr. Prlic himself during your preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I have not. I have not seen -- I have not met him over the last couple of years, but I, you know, discussed with others. Those who are listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, Akmadzic, Backovic, Gotovusa, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You know Mr. -- or Dr. Prlic I should say, from your IMF days as you've already indicated in your testimony when you were working initially in Warsaw just prior to the end of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were actually my -- the World Bank days because I never worked for the IMF.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's the time when I met him. Actually, I think Mr. Tomic introduced me to him in one of the first visits in Sarajevo because he was at that time minister of foreign affairs, if I'm not mistaken, of the Federation. So we were not dealing with the minister of foreign affairs much, we were dealing mainly with the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Economy. So I was not dealing with him allot but I know of him, yes, and I met him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your direct testimony, you actually drew our attention to a page in that World Bank country study, and you can look at it if you wish, it's the acknowledgement section on page Roman numeral vii in which the World Bank was acknowledging with thanks various people who were involved in the preparation of this report. Do you recall taking us to that page?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And as you've indicated, Dr. Prlic is listed on that page, also Neven Tomic, I believe you pointed that out. I noticed that one of the other people whom you've later interviewed as part of this report for this trial is Mr. Backovic, Enver --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- Backovic who was involved in the economic situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you -- apart from the interview of Neven Tomic, which you indicate occurred on the 20th of October 2007, did you have any further consultations or dealing with Mr. Tomic as part of your preparation of this report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. Most of the discussion we had then that -- at that very moment, but I read -- I read his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. That was my next question. His testimony in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just from last month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I received some of the, you know, testimonies in preparation for this one, so I, you know, went to see it more from the point of view how does it look to be testifying -- for those who heard Mr. Primorac testimony, so I read some of those testimonies in order to kind of, you know, see, you know, okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- how does it look being here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the Defence for Mr. Prlic made Mr. Tomic's testimony available to you after he testified in this case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents were provided to me by the Defence, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Anyone else whose testimony -- well, actually that will take me to my next question. I'm -- your report is dated from October of 2007, so that's for my understanding sort of the end point of any testimony that you might have reviewed in making the report, and so now can we understand that in addition, you reviewed the subsequent testimony of Mr. Tomic which came after this report was finalise?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, October of 2008 is the date of when I finished the report. Before the report, I looked into the testimony of one of the witnesses on these sections, I looked into the Primorac testimony, I believe. And yes, after that in preparation for my coming here, I was -- it was suggested to me that I see and I read the Tomic testimony for my preparation once the report was finalized and also especially because at that time we were discussing how to prepare this PowerPoint presentation. So the idea was to how to summarise what is in the report so that you know, we could really in a short time present the most important findings of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. There are a couple of other witnesses whom you interviewed as part of your preparation of the report who are also came and testified in this case. One of those is Mile Akmadzic. Did you read Mr. Akmadzic's testimony in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I have not read Mr. Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, you indicate in your report that among - it was my impression, you'll correct me if I'm wrong - some of the earlier initial documentation you were provided was the testimony of Dr. Ciril Ribicic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
