utterances.text: Not the testimony, but I read --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me, if I could just take you through it step by step, I think ultimately we'll get there. The testimony -- that was my question, you said in your report you read his testimony. It wasn't clear to me whether his testimony was from this case or another case.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Well, I read the testimony and also I met Mr. Ribicic because, you know, he is a Slovenian and we know each other and basically --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, maybe I didn't ask the question correctly. Which testimony did you read or did you read both Dr. Ribicic's testimony from this trial or was it from an earlier trial or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. It was so many different document. But Mr. Ribicic what I think is -- certainly I am aware of his testimony because we were discussing before and after his testimony both his book and his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you've read his testimony from any cases, there are only two in which he testified in this Tribunal, you are aware, sir, that Dr. Ribicic prepared an expert report himself that was submitted as part of these proceedings, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you read the report? And I know there is a book that may or may not conform exactly to the report, I don't know. So I'm more interested in the report that Dr. Ribicic submitted as part of his testimony. Did you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know, I read all these languages, you know, so I read certainly, you know, the book, you know, in which he is of course referring to a lot of documents and somehow summarising the report. But what exactly -- then I also read some English versions of different documents. So was that a report or was that, you know, English translation of the book, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. The book that I believe you are referring to is English title is "Genesis of One Misconception ." Is that the book you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Genesis of One Misconception," [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, from reading the book and reading his testimony, I take it you are familiar with or at least aware of the various opinions and conclusions that Dr. Ribicic has reached based on his review of the documentation, his consideration of the activities of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I was reading his book and when I was discussing with him, I lacked documents. He is a lawyer and so he was looking at it from a different angle than I did. I looked into the economic documents and I looked into the events from the economic point of view. So clearly when we were discussing, and he's, you know, a Slovenian constitutional lawyer --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, he's a Slovenian constitutional judge, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, yes. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It's a small difference to those of us who are lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- apologise. Yes. He is a judge at the Slovene Constitutional Court. A court of constitution matters in Republic of Slovenia. So whenever being an economist never discuss back home with lawyers, you know, opinions, but I was just discussing with him, okay, how did -- how did he prepare for that work, what kind of, you know, issues were that involved. And you know, I read his book, but you know, I missed in this -- I was actually surprised after reading his book and after being, you know, presented with all these documents that he had been analysing so little set of documents. Especially because when I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. And I should -- I should just say at this stage which is still rather early in the cross-examination, it's a cross-examination. Mr. Karnavas very correctly allowed you to present to the Trial Chamber your report that things that you thought should be emphasized, et cetera. Cross-examination is a bit different, and under the time constraints that I have to operate under, I have a number of topics and issues that I need to raise with you. So if I cut you off, I hope you will accept that I'm not intending any disrespect, but I am going to have to insist to try to bring you back to the point that I'm hoping to get to. And I think between -- if we both try to work together on that we'll get there. I don't want to limit you to yes or no answers, but at the same time I am going to try to keep you a little more focused on my own questions.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine, but I would of course like to use the opportunity to explain my opinion so that the honoured judges would be able to understand my yes or no, yes with but or no with no, just.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Sure. I totally accept that. You started to talk about what it was that Dr. Ribicic reviewed and it struck me there were some similarity. You had very viewed the legislation of Herceg-Bosna or at least the legislation that relates to issues such as those that you've testified about and Dr. Ribicic did the same; that is, if you recall from his testimony, he read all of the legislation of the Narodni list, the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna. So in that respect, the universe or the scope of the documentation is the same. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because certainly he did not read the two of the documents which I had -- at least he was not aware of them, this is the World Bank study and the IMF study.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm talking about the Narodni list, the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna, if you'll just stick with me, that's something that you each of you have read, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the Official Gazette usually with the particular law has an explanation, and then it has also if you want the reasoning why particular article has been appointed as it was, and usually there are also then reports by the executive authority explaining what they were doing under the particular issues. But for as I have said, when I was discussing this with him - and this is -- I'm just explaining to you what I was discussing with him during my -- even before my decision to accept the job, I tried to of course from him to find actually two questions. Was he just limiting himself to the Official Gazettes or did he, you know, have actually been there or visited some of the people or whether he was reading something what I personally had been involved in 1994, 1996 which I believe he was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may just make a short interjection here. Counsel is suggesting that this gentleman knows exactly what Dr. Ribicic read, and I don't think that there is a basis for that. In fact we don't know exactly what he read. If he wants -- if he wishes to point to the transcript and we can see a list of the documents, but to suggest that they both read the identical same thing is rather speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I'm just suggesting that both of them read the Narodni list decisions of Herceg-Bosna. I don't think it's terribly controversial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My point is I don't know whether Dr. Ribicic read all of what this gentleman read, and I think it was -- at one point there was an exchange where I believe it was you, Judge Trechsel, that pointed out that there was a lot of material that he didn't have to read all of it. Of course, that exchange dealt with presidential transcripts. I mean, I vividly recall of my cross-examination of the gentleman. But my point is, to get this particular witness to vouch as far as what Dr. Ribicic read is calling for speculation, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Another or a similarity if you will that struck me or appeared to me from your report as well as the one prepared by Dr. Ribicic was that both of you appear to have conducted your analysis in phases. You indicated that - and you have repeatedly referred to the three phases if I've got to correctly - in respect of Herceg-Bosna, the early sort of local oriented or dominated phase, if I may put it that way, you'll correct me, in which there was a presidency operating in Herceg-Bosna. A second phase in which there was an executive authority, the HVO. And then the third phase in the latter part of 1993 and beyond where there was the Croatian republic with its House of Representatives. Are you aware that Dr. Ribicic also conducted an analysis that distinguished between those phases in the life the Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I would like to -- of course when I talk about the first phase in Herceg-Bosna -- this sector or phase which is also the first phase in the post-war development in all local communities. And what I am not aware of, whether Mr. Ribicic had looked also what was happening in other local communities throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina and whether he was looking into the some of the decisions at the level of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina such as decree law on covering the social needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But my question was about the phases and the approach of the phases within Herceg-Bosna. Would you agree with me that his approach was -- or your approach was similar to the one that he used? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I mean I know -- I don't know how he undertook his analysis, I only know from what he was saying to me that he received a bunch of documents and then, you know, presented this book which, you know, is his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, of course a fundamental difference between your work and the work of Dr. Ribicic and you've already alluded to it is the fact that your perspective here is the economic sphere whereas Dr. Ribicic's analysis is in a different sphere, that being the legal and constitutional aspect. Would you agree that that is a fundamental difference in your approach?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was looking into the analysis of the economic measures. In the context of the overall economic environment in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was looking into the measures and activities as an economist from the economic point of view. And as I have said, I looked it from the point of view of the fact that that was war economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And so in reviewing all of the documents from any of the municipalities or areas, you -- is it correct to say you did not consider the legality of any given decree or decision issued at a municipal level or a regional level, rather you, if I can put it this way, took that for granted or you didn't concern yourself with the legality of the legislation, rather you were more interested in simply what were they doing or what were they attempting to do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would disagree with you. I started with the Yugoslav constitution and the constitution of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was at that time valid. And I also started to look whether in the basic presidency decree with the function of the law issues like war budget, issues like provision for being able to issue new fiscal regulation was put in place. And I have seen that in 1992 that was actually allowed. I even say in the report that when I then -- to my surprise actually identified these presidency decree on the law -- presidency decree with the powers of the law on the so-called districts, I have seen a lot of basis for legally correct measures being undertaken by first local communities, and then also region-wide authorities. So I did not forget about legality. But I'm not a lawyer, I'm, you know, an economist, but you know, I have in my previous work, I have written a couple of laws, Bank of Slovenia Law, Banking Law, Law on Procurement of Slovenia Public Finance, Act of Slovenia, so I know what is the notion of having, you know, the primacy of the laws and how a particular law decree shall be based upon. And that's why always very detailed looked into the preamble and of the explanation of a particular measure. So yes, I was not looking solely from -- I did not look at in the same manner as maybe he did it, but I certainly have taken into account whether a particular measure which was undertaken at the level of local communities and later at the level of the wider region, had an appropriate legal backing. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, okay I think you've given us a sufficient enough answer on that. Let me put it to you more specifically. For example in reviewing a decree or a decision issued by the HVO municipality, the municipal HVO, did you consider whether or not the HVO, the municipal HVO in Mostar, was the lawful body to issue such a decision under the laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific, which decision you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. We'll get to that. I've got a number to show you -- a number of those to show you. You're aware, are you not, sir, that Dr. Ribicic, based on his review of the Herceg-Bosna legislation drew a distinction between that legislation and the laws and the constitution in Slovenia in respect of the treatment of minorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the line of questioning. First of all, we are not here -- this gentleman was not called here in order to either support or attack Dr. Ribicic's report, which if we all recall relied extensively on one presidential transcript of the 27th December 1991. Dr. Ribicic has nothing to do with this particular report. And what he says about Slovenia or anything else is irrelevant. And it's well beyond the scope of the direct examination or the purpose of this particular report. So on the grounds of relevancy, I would ask for a ruling at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can respond, the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the relevance, what is your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The witness has in his report and throughout his testimony made reference to the constitutional role of municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina under the constitution, in times of war, in times of peace. Now, he has also obviously made a number of conclusions and opinions based upon the activities of the municipalities. The relevance of -- or the weight of those opinions is based not only on what he knows and what he says, but also what he doesn't say and what he does not consider. And it's our submission that the weight of this to be given this report is effected significantly by the factor or the question whether or not the witness considered the legality or the lawfulness of the bodies that are issuing the various decrees. If they are unlawful bodies that are issuing the various decrees, then that is a point that bears upon ultimately the conclusions that he is reaching in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may briefly reply, where is it in the transcript or in the report where Dr. Ribicic looked at the constitution and particularly to the provisions, to the provisions that this gentleman cites in his report as a basis of what was happening all over in all the municipalities, Muslim or Croat dominated municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's nothing. Now we are trying to bootstrap somehow Dr. Ribicic, who was discredited in my opinion both as a scholar, as a judge, or as a witness, in order to and to somehow support his testimony by cross-examining an economist. It's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking him to support or deny or to deny the testimony. What I'm trying to do is to simply to draw the distinction between what this witness has looked at and what Dr. Ribicic has looked at and how their conclusions may then diverge on the basis of their different roles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But there's -- Your Honour, it's not a dispute that one was a constitutional quote unquote expert. Here we have an economist. They have looked at it from two different angles. How can you possibly have now cross-examination and say, Well, a constitutional expert looked at it this way and you are not. That wasn't the purpose of the report. So I don't see how you can mix apples and oranges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the purpose of the witness's report is a report based on economic considerations that turned on the basis of what I understood that seek to demonstrate that in place the players on the ground were faced with such a situation that prompted them to take a series of measures via decrees, via text of law that had consequences possibly political but at any rate human on the fate of the inhabitants of these localities, and on that basis I'm given to understand that the Defence counsel via this expert witness seeks to demonstrate that contrary to your argument on the joint criminal enterprise that there was another approach which the reasons of survival, economic, et cetera, that's what the Defence seeks to bring out. You are now cross-examining it and trying to -- via the Ribicic expert to claim that this expert witness has reached conclusions without taking account of constitutional, legal, or other data. You are both in a different area; Defence in the economic sphere, now you are returning to the legal sphere. Put your questions and the Judges will determine. What counts, in my view, is what the witness will answer to your questions as to know what is within or without the scope. We'll see that at the end of the day. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think I can -- I'll try to wrap this up with one last question, which is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As counsel has pointed out and as you've already indicated there was a constitutional analysis done by Dr. Ribicic, one by you done in the economic sphere. Are we to understand that in your view because of your background, because of your focus, your report and your findings are based strictly on the economic sphere, without regard to the constitutional legal framework conducted by Dr. Ribicic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. And how can he possibly answer that question? What -- I mean, this is total nonsense. Look -- Your Honours, read the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, your expert witness is someone, and it's not the first time, who has held important responsibilities. He is currently Chief of Staff to the government. Well, as Chief of Staff, obviously has minimal constitutional and political knowledge. So if the question is incomprehensible to him, well the expert -- your expert witness will say, I can't answer that, but if he can answer that please let him answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is really, if I could use one of the often phrases, how often do -- when did you stop beating your wife type of a question, how can you possibly answer that question. Again, we are mixing apples and oranges, we are not here to attack Dr. Ribicic. We have done that already. We are not doing it through Mr. Cvikl. So I don't understand the basis of this question. And Your Honour, with all due respect, I'm not here for my good looks. Occasionally I'm called upon to make an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understand the question. Perhaps the expert can't answer in which case he will say I can't answer. If he can answer he'll answer, if not he won't answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way, I'll try to rephrase it in a way that is perhaps is less controversial. You are not a lawyer, you are not a constitutional lawyer. You have no comment on Dr. Ribicic's report from a substantive point of view in terms of the conclusions and opinions; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have my own view on that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have not been asked, I have not been asked by -- to do this analysis to make a view on that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. And that's because you are not qualified to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I was asked to present the economic measures and developments and within that I looked into the legislation. And I looked into in the legislation from the point of view of what local communities were either authorised to do it or they have done that in the circumstances prevailing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you are not qualified to look into Dr. Ribicic's report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm qualified to look into it because I was surprised, surprised in his report, and his analysis to look into documents for which now I will quote, he had said, Everything on the outside looks perfect, but behind there were some agenda. And I have not seen that agenda. Because I was looking into the report from an economic point of view. If there would be an agenda, there would be no borders established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would be no borders established on the southern border of what at that time was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And that's why I have asked Mr. Ribicic when we were discussing that well before he came here and well after his book was already published whether he had looked in what the IMF and the World Bank were finding in the 1994, 1996 period, and did he not confirm that to me. So I was quite surprised that he had not looked into these documents because those documents explain that what we have seen in 1994 to 1996 period in these very --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, we know what you have seen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. He is entitled to the full answer of that question. It was open ended and he should be aware of that. Now, he has asked about Dr. Ribicic, he is getting it now. He is entitled to that entire answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I asked if he was qualified. He thinks he's qualified. I'll take that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Stringer, let the witness complete -- please let him complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. So I was quite surprised in discussing with him that he had not looked into some of the documents that the World Bank and the IMF prepared and he is describing that period. And that he had not looked into the fact that the banking system, the financial system, had been established there, and that he had not looked into the fact what was happening particular areas under the authority of the local municipality with the Bosniak majority. And that's all what I could say about this book. This book has been for me a surprise. Even before I was start looking into document because it did not recall what I've seen when I visited this country in 1994, 1996. And what I've seen there, I've seen three different economies. A vibrant economy in the Herceg-Bosna, in Tuzla, and I've seen a lack of the measures at the level of the central government authorities, those measures that I was part of preparing when I was economist during the independence of time. And Mr. Ribicic should be aware of this, that all of those measures that were -- have been undertaken and should be undertaken were not undertaken by the central government authorities of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they had this difficult economic situation. And as I have explained yesterday to The Honours here, if a war in Slovenia would prevail for more than two week, for let's say 6 months or 9 months, and we would see in the eastern part of Slovenia free territory, and the free territory would have to of course ensure economic survival of the population in this very area, the type of the measures would be very similar. And that would be of course completely valid because according to the Slovene constitution, according to the Bosnia constitution, according to the Yugoslav constitution, that's what a socio-political community of Opstina were authorised to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Cvikl, in your report you indicated that the purpose of the analysis is to hopefully provide the Judges with an understanding appreciation of the HVO's efforts and intentions in the economic sphere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, in attempting to inform the Judges of the HVO's efforts and intentions, it's true, is it not, first of all, that you were not in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war. You were not there during 1991, 1992, or 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with all due respect, when I was there in --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm asking you, it's true, isn't it, that you were not in Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1991, 1992 or 1993? That's a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991 to 1993 period I was not there, but I was in the region, I was working with the World Bank on countries in the area, and I was informed a lot of what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were living in Washington DC during that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I lived in Washington DC but 160 days out of 365 days I was in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was still part before the independence of Yugoslavia, and we were -- while we were trying to organise --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you what you were doing, I just asked you where you were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was Sarajevo May 1991, or else it was Belgrade May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1992 and 1993 I was not in -- physically in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand correctly, 1994 you were doing work in Warsaw and meeting with people from Bosnia-Herzegovina because it wasn't yet safe to go into Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not able to travel in Bosnia-Herzegovina but we were meeting authorities from Bosnia-Herzegovina coming to Warsaw Rezda [phoen] mission with documents and presenting the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So in 1992 and 1993 then, you were based or living in Washington, DC working as a consultant with the World Bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was an economist with the World Bank. I was not hired consultant, I was regular staff. I was elected in the generation 1991 young professionals, one of 32 among 5.000 candidates, so I was the what is called regular staff of the World Bank and I was not one of the consultants coming in and out, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You -- were you at this time studying, I saw in your CV that you were studying or at one point in a PhD programme at Florida State University, when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was 1989 [Realtime transcript read in error "1999"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever complete your studies or obtain your PhD?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the system, the Yugoslav --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, that's a yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you attain a PhD from Florida state university where you were studying for is my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: My studies at the Florida State University were in accordance and in agreement with between the National Bank of Yugoslavia and the Florida State University in exchange of American Yugoslav scholars. And that studies, the PhD studies, were the basis for me in the 1990 obtain what is known in Slovene so-called Skony [phoen] system, the postgraduate studies, the degree called Master of Science. Is that a PhD in American standards or is this PhD in European Bologna, that is a dispute that goes on for years. But yes, I took at the Florida State University post so-called doctor -- doctor studies at the so-called Department of Social Science and Economics, and I was there preparing a model on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I am sorry you can't finish. I asked you a simple question about when you studied, when you obtained your PhD. I'm sorry, and with all respect Mr. Cvikl, I don't have time and frankly we are not interested in what you were working on when you were at Florida State University.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying -- I'm trying to explain to you that the six months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm giving you a little speech which I have given to numerous witness, and I apologise to all others in the courtroom who have heard this many times. You are in an uncomfortable situation. I have been in that situation once too, so I can really sympathize. According to the rules in cross-examination counsel, in this case for the Prosecution, can ask you questions which are pointed to a yes or no answer. And you may feel the need and the desire to comment rather than say yes or no. But Mr. Karnavas has, I don't know how many times he repeated when he cross-examined that his questions had the answer yes, no, I don't remember, I forgotten, something like that. I don't know. And this is a rule of the game which is very tough on you. But I am sure that you are a man of great knowledge and understanding and I would invite you kindly to comply with this rule even if it is sometimes disagreeable and you would like to explain more. Because as Mr. Stringer says, his time indeed is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: One clarification for the record, Your Honour, I believe it should say on line 16 page 61, "1989" as opposed to "1999." Unless I'm incorrect and perhaps that could be clarified as far as when he attended. The transcript said 1999, I believe that's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question. After Mr. Stringer's question on Washington, you were then in the World Bank, you said that you went to the -- you spent 160 days in the area but you were not there all the time, that you spent half of your time in Washington which is understandable. But underlying that question, there is a more general one. Can one draft a report when one has not been in situ? So based on that, those who work at the World Bank, you did work at the World Bank, today somebody is working is based in Washington, is working on the economy of Sudan. I guess that even if that person is not in Sudan, from Washington he has available a horde of documents so that if he works on that country, the work he is about to do for the World Bank should be faultless. Is that the way it works or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the way the things works in the World Bank you are an economist for a particular country, you collect and you work all the time on that particular country, either by travelling to country or by following through the available information, information that should be provided to you by authorities on that country. And that exactly what I was doing from 1994 where I was appointed economist for Bosnia-Herzegovina and actually is the first World Bank economist because before we did not undertake any economic work on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as I understand it you were the number one, the world expert on this because there was never anyone before you and you were the first, is that the way things should be understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Following the collapse of former Yugoslavia, there were six new members that inherited the seat of Yugoslavia and I was first. The first World Bank economist for the former Yugoslavia republic of Macedonia, 1992, 1994 period. On the basis of that work, a couple of reports were prepared but most important the first economic recovery loan, I was asked by then the head of the regional department, and he had decided that among all economists that he had in his team, he would ask me to be first World Bank economist for Bosnia-Herzegovina, most likely for two reasons, for the good work which I did for Macedonia, from my past experience in Slovenia, and also for the fact that I was able to confer and read documents that others only need yet to be translated for them, and that's how we started the work in 1994, 1996 period. And that work I believe continued for the World Bank point of view successfully and for that and other -- I also got the World Bank award for excellence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that this question shed some light on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President it caused me to go back to the World Bank report which is 1D 02967, the one dated June 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this earlier, Mr. Cvikl, the acknowledgements. Now, in respect of this report at least, first sentence indicates the report, this is page Roman numeral vi on the World Bank report, 1D 02967. Now, in respect of this report, sir, it appears to me that your capacity here was as a consultant as opposed to a staff member of the World Bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. The centre says the bank staff and consultants included and then it goes by alphabetical orders, Sebnem Akkaya, she was consultant; Emily Andrews, consultant; and Michael Borish, World Bank staff; myself, World Bank staff; William Fox, I believe he was World Bank staff; et cetera; and Sweder van Wijnbergen was World Bank staff, now he was then the state secretary here in the Ministry of Finance of the Netherlands. So does not distinguish between the staff and the consultants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You need to try to speak more slowly, especially when you are reading.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You can put that aside, Mr. Cvikl. Getting back to what I was asking about before about -- you are not being present in the Bosnia-Herzegovina or in the former Yugoslavia during 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. I was in former Yugoslavia because I was often travelling to the former Yugoslavian Republic of Macedonia which was at that time the territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of Yugoslavia, and I travelled a lot to Slovenia, I travelled a lot to Croatia, so I was in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your personal knowledge of the efforts and intentions of the HVO, which is what you address here, in fact you have none, isn't that correct? Everything that you know about the HVO, its efforts and intentions as set out in your report is based upon the things you've read, the things you've been told?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's based on the visits to the region as well. In the 1995 and in the 1996 still practically, just before the Dayton agreement when we were travelling there we were meeting authorities of HVO. I was meeting -- sorry, I was meeting HVO Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna customs officers all the way up to May -- sorry, March of 1996 at the border crossings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your knowledge about the efforts, intentions of the HVO during 1992 and 1993 is based upon things you read and things you were told by others; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly that is based on the opinion which the team of the World Bank and the IMF have been provided with in the 1994, 1996 period when we were able to have direct meetings with the authorities, and on the basis of the documents not just issued by the HVO, but also issued by the central government authorities of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and local municipalities in the Muslim or Bosniak controls and the Croat majority area and on the basis of interviews which I have had.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphones be brought -- put closer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So again, what you know about the efforts and intentions of the HVO is based upon the things you read and the things you were told because you weren't there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would repeat again, in 1995, 1996 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me you don't need to repeat your answer if you are just going to say again what you've already said. I tried to ask you a yes or no question. Everything you know about the efforts and intentions of the HVO from 1992 and 1993 is based upon the things you read and the things you were told by others; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the things which I observed by myself during visits in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And the same holds true, does it not, for your statements and your conclusions to the extent they are based on the fact that the central government in Sarajevo was cut off and was not functioning? What you say about that and the extent to which the central government was cut off, your knowledge of that is based again on things you've read, things you've been told by others, because you were not there and you don't know that personally based on your own experience?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. My personal experience of my first travel to Sarajevo, the Mount Igman, Mount Igman, in year 1995 was for me clearly a proof how difficult was to get in and out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the extent to which your report is based upon 1992, 1993, that your conclusions there are again based upon what you've read and what you've been told by others because you weren't there and you did not experience that yourself; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993 it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. You don't have any personal knowledge about the extent to which that changed, say, from April of 1992 at the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout the remainder of 1992 and throughout 1993? You don't know to what extent that Sarajevo's being cut off may have changed or may have been altered based upon the various events that were taking place; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your report is based upon the premise that the Sarajevo central government had collapsed, was cut off from the rest of the country and could not operate. Are we to understand that that premise remains in effect throughout the entire period of time of your report, throughout all of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even at the time of 1995 when we were first coming into Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have not seen institutions up and running that were important or that should be there and would enable the control to be effective for effective implementation of the measures by the central government. I have not seen in 1995 operational republican-wide Social Accounting Office, banking institutions, insurance institutions, at the central government level. We have only seen when we came there in 1995 situation where we could not even use Bosnian dinar in Sarajevo itself but we had to use Deutschemark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not transfer funds into Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm asking you about your knowledge of how cut off central government was, I'll ask you about currency later.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- well, the central government --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you another question. Based on what you've just said then, is it your testimony, sir, that in your view, the central government in Sarajevo, central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was just as cut off from the rest of the country in 1995 as it was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would from my experience up to the point that KFOR or IFOR at that time.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was SFOR IFOR -- I believe it was IFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: SFOR is later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it was up to the time that IFOR actually entered into Sarajevo, the central government authority were quite cut off, and I will explain this: That in February 1996, we could not rely on the central government authority to assure protection of the international donor's conference by the government. We had to ask IFOR to undertake these measures. So effective government institutions were not up and running. We could not travel. We are Hadzici [phoen] just with the support of the central government authorities we had to ask IFOR. So the institutions that were available to the republican institutions as far as I'm concerned were even in the February 1996 were not in control of the whole territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right and do you know to what extent that level of control was different than was the situation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I was looking into the economic issues, certainly the payment system, the payment system, the social accounting office, the collection of taxes, tax administration, the monetary system, the banking, the financial system, and basis for operations of enterprises at the -- throughout whole Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Actually, throughout the whole Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was not possible in 1995. Of course, it must be better than it was 1992, but this Federation-wide institutions were not yet there. I would like to just tell that even the exchange of the funds between the Social Accounting Offices was happening immediately by cash and that was invention by the IMF economic team and by the World Bank long after we came into the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough unless the Judges want to hear more. Mr. Cvikl, do you know to what extent Sarajevo remained cut off from Herceg-Bosna throughout 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my understanding there was a possibility for the people, and that's what was explained to me by the people that came out to -- out of Sarajevo to visit us in February 1994, that there was a possibility for people going via tunnel and then later via Mount of Igman to the area south of Sarajevo. And also the first visitors from central government actually brought documents, and I would just like here to explain a small detail. They brought documents in rucksacks, in carry bags, and since there was water in that tunnel, when we met them in Sarajevo, in Warsaw, they asked for iron in order to with iron get water out of the documents because otherwise the documents were -- so there were difficulties for central government authorities to even depart Sarajevo, and I don't know how much they were really in control of Herceg-Bosna or the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So based on what you've said, your knowledge -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go back to the 1992, 1993 period because the Prosecutor was asking you what your knowledge was of that period. It is important also to know what you know exactly. I confess that I did not know what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, but unlike me, you, you were a member of the former Yugoslavia. So you must be much more aware than any westerner who didn't know what was happening then. When you were in Washington, did you keep yourself informed of what was happening in the former Yugoslavia, in Croatia, in Slovenia, in Macedonia? Were there newspapers, were you interested in that or did that escape you altogether?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was very much informed about that. As I have said, I have been half a year, at least a half working days of the year outside Washington, mostly working in Macedonia, and I was also receiving a couple of newspapers back from Slovenia into Washington. There were a lot of reports what is going on. Plus I was visiting Bosnia-Herzegovina extensively before departing to Washington, and I have seen what we had to do in Slovenia in 1990, 1991 for independence, and I've seen what happened in two-weeks war and information on the military situation, and these facts of, you know, how many of the country is occupied, et cetera, were for me an indication that there is a war economy out there as confirmed later by the documents which we had received on the energy collapse, 90 percent drop of industrial production, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the World Bank for the people working, the experts working for the World Bank, do they have some kind of press review or press releases from news agencies, AFB, or other that is would be distributed to the offices and to the staff members so that per region the staff members could read the information? Is that the way it was working then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That type of information I was getting -- some of the information I was getting by myself through the newspaper which I was receiving. Some of them I was getting via the Slovenian embassy. And then there are a lot of different press releases by the, you know, press office of the World Bank, plus we were all at that time very much reading what was Oxford Analytica, doing Oxford Analytica doing on that. So we were reading all this, you know, news from the region. And I being an economist in the Europe, EC 2 country operation, European department, we were responsible for the whole Yugoslavia, so we were informed on things as they were developing and we knew that in 1992, 1993 situation was such that we could not even start the economic work on Bosnia-Herzegovina despite the fact that we knew that country was not paying dues on the World Bank loans and that the problem for us is piling up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. You were working in the section Europe C 2, did your head of service have organised theme-related meetings on the relevant issues, for example, for the former Yugoslavia, did you have briefings or feedback sessions about the situation be it the economic or military situation? Is that the way you work at the World Bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way we -- the team that work in Slovenia. I could not work on Slovenia because I'm citizen of Slovenia. The team working on Croatia which was already at that time up and running team, and the team which works on Macedonia, we were working closely together. And especially the team working on Croatia which was a kind of working closely with us was of help when we started the work on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to stop asking questions, we could go on but maybe there are other things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I'm told it's time for the break. I can continue, it's as you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For 10 minutes, you know, once we are right in full swing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've been working for close to 2 hours. I mean, time flies, I didn't notice. Maybe we should have a break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in session. Before I ask Mr. Stringer to proceed, the Trial Chamber just learned a few minutes ago that the Petkovic Defence has just filed a 12-page request for review or alternatively a certification for appeal of our oral decision of the 12th of January. The Trial Chamber therefore request the parties to express their views by Friday. The Trial Chamber will hand down an oral or written decision prior to the beginning of the cross-examination of Mr. Davor Marijan. His examination-in-chief is scheduled to start on Monday at 2.15. So please do file your positions by Friday. We are going to continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, I want to take you back to your testimony from yesterday, the 13th of January, you were responding to a question from Judge Antonetti, and you said, and this is on page 35260 starting at line 23: "I have said earlier, Your Honours, regarding the presidency of Bosnia ..." -- excuse me "... regarding the presidency of Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina decree on districts, we will get to it. Maybe it would be appropriate to put in the preamble also that this decree, but then of course that decree puts local communities together in a different manner than was done by the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and that the way the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna local community were put together was really depending on what was the -- you know, what were the military activities took place." And I want to ask you a couple of questions about your views in terms of the selection or the establishment of the local communities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and what I'd like to do is I'm going to show you a couple of documents, take you to some parts of them. We won't talk about them, and then after we've looked at both documents, then we'll be able to have our discussion. So the first document I'd like to take you to, Mr. Cvikl, is P 00070, and that is in -- it's in the separate documents you have there in front of you. Now, 00070, this is the conclusions of a joint meeting of the Herzegovina regional community and the Travnik regional community. It's dated the 12th of November 1991 at the end. You see it appears over the names of Mate Boban and Daria Koric, and these are the conclusions of the joint meeting of these two regional communities. It's rather early, 12 November 1991. First question is, have you ever seen this before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. You'll see under the conclusions, there's a first paragraph, and this states that: "These two regional communities remain of the opinion stated in the conclusions adopted at earlier meetings that the Croatian people of this region and all of Bosnia-Herzegovina still support the unanimously accepted orientation and conclusions adopted in agreements with president Franjo Tudjman in June of 1991 in Zagreb?" And then it continues: "On the basis of the conclusions of the above-mentioned meetings and in agreement in Zagreb, as well as separate conclusions," which you see are referred to there. "These two regional communities have unanimously decided that the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally embrace a determined enact of policy which will realise our eternal dream, a common Croatian state." And then it continues: "In order that historic goal may soon also be a reality, these two regional communities ask that legal and political documents be prepared and published proclaiming a Croatian banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina and a holding of a referendum on joining the Republic of Croatia as the first steps on the road to the final solution of the Croatia question..." and it continues. The next document then - and we'll come back to both these to talk about them - the next document is P 00302, and that is in binder number 1. While you were reaching for that Mr. Cvikl, I can just inform you, this is a decision on establishing the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yeah. And we've all seen this document. I take it you've seen this document also?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So are you familiar with that one, 302, are you familiar with that or do we need to walk through it a little bit? I mean, you've discussed it in your report. It's among the documents that were provided to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen this document, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, the third thing I want to take you to, and then we'll talk about this. It's not a document, it's some testimony, and I'm going to read it to you. It's a testimony of another person who testified in this case, and his name was Zoran Buntic, and Mr. Buntic was the head of the justice department of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And he testified in this trial and I'm going to read you just a little excerpt from his testimony. It's on page 30870 of the transcript. And this is a question that I put to him: "Given that the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina were a constituent nation, given the demographic trends in which their numbers were diminishing, is it your view that the Croatian people should have had an area that they could govern themselves so that they wouldn't have to be worried about being outvoted all the time by another group, by another constituent nation?" And his answer was: "That's correct. I answered such questions in the course of my evidence and I entirely stand" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- and he goes on to continue, he qualifies that as having been his own personal opinion. But what we were talking about there was reference or was languages that's found in 302, the decision establishing Herceg-Bosna in the preamble or the reasons section in which they cite the unacceptability of the unitary state model in multi-ethnic societies. That's about halfway down the third paragraph on the section on reasons, do you see that? "Pursuant to the unacceptability of the unitary state model in multi-ethnic societies." All right. Now, based on that, this is what I have to ask you, did you consider in your report, because as you've indicated, you were attempting again from an economic point of view to determine what were the efforts and the intentions of the HVO. My question is whether you considered the possibility that the political leadership of Herceg-Bosna actually had another objective, a political objective, which was to create a territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina that it could attach to Croatia eventually or which might stay within Bosnia-Herzegovina but which would be organised in a separate way, a different way than this unitary state model that was in effect in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me object to the question, at least at one predicate. At that time Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a unitary state. That was Alija Izetbegovic's dream, to make it a unitary state. It was based on the constitution. You had three constituent nations as well as other national minorities living in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was never ever, ever a unitary state at that point in time. So if the question could be rephrased, I have no objection. But that last part is a fact that is not in evidence and is totally historically incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Well, your objection has been recorded, but what you say, Mr. Karnavas, is in the text, so you are raising an objection on something that is enshrined in the text. I mean, I don't mind objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Bosnia-Herzegovina was not a unitary state. Alija Izetbegovic was trying to make it into one. The whole point of the war was because all of the other republics did not want to have a unitary state. I think the gentleman can answer the question, but I think to suggest that at that point in time the constitution had changed to the effect that the Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina no longer enjoyed a constituent status as well as the Serbs or the Muslims as they were known back then or Bosniaks is incorrect. You had three constituent nations in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a speech, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've had this debate before. All this has been recorded, the judges are aware of the problem. Let's move ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, you ought to withdraw the words that was in effect, because there you go beyond what's in the text here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, there is another problem as well. It is not that the question is somehow out of the frame of real facts on the ground which Mr. Karnavas said. But it is also highly speculative. It is -- the actually the witness is asked to speculate. The question, the major parties or which might stay within Bosnia-Herzegovina. He doesn't know that. He, as he testified, he was looking at the document to see whether there is from the aspect of economical and fiscal expert. So he is not interested in other possible explanations. The Prosecutor should be interested in other possible explanations of reasons, but that should have been done before the trial, not now, before the indictment. I don't think that this witness is expert --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, if the witness can't answer, he will say so, and if is he speculating he will say so as well. So basically at first glance there's no reason to believe that the witness would speculate. And if he does, we'll see that. The witness is supposed to give exact answers to exact questions. If the question is speculative, that may happen, then he will answer speculatively to a speculative question. Go ahead, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You've heard all the objections and the comments, I'll try to rephrase my question again. I'll take you back to the testimony of Mr. Buntic. He agreed that -- in his view the Croatian people should have an area that they could govern themselves so they that wouldn't have to worry about being outvoted by another group. The document from 12 November 1991 talks about declaration of banovina area and joining that territory to Croatia. I'll ask the question again. Hypothetically, if those indeed were political objectives of the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, you did not consider that in performing your analysis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer without interruption. First I would like of course saying that the preamble in the decision on the establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the way I read it is true. Pursuant to the unacceptability of the unitarian state model in a multi-ethnic society they have decided to do something. Here I would like of course first to say that because of the unacceptability of the unitarian state model that was supposed to be at the whole level of Yugoslavia the country collapsed. That is number one. Second, I would hypothetically speculate that if they really wanted to do what you are suggesting, they should do nothing. They should simply sit back and there should be no activity either by the local communities or by the region-wide communities because there would be no borders and there would be, as I've said yesterday, economically the territory of the Croatian majority areas economically sooner or later be economically part of the wider region so --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I actually asked you a different question which was, if in fact this was a political objective, you did not consider that possibility in making your report; is that correct or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my report is analysis of the economic measures within the economic environment that was at that time in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen that economically speaking there was 50 or 100 small local economic areas were to be created. These recognition was a recognition even by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's why they issued this decree on the districts, and economically there was a need to reconnect those independent economic areas for the benefit of the population. And I have not been looking into the economic measures from the point of view what would be then, if you want, ultimate intention. But I would of course as an economist argue and also argue on the basis of what were experienced in the region that if you want to integrate this territory into the Republic of Croatia, one would simply do nothing but would let economic integration to take place. And that would be easily done, it would be much more difficult and it was much more difficult to do the opposite. To create borders, to create schooling systems in the -- this territory, to create all these measures that enable the survival of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. So I have your answer, which is as you've indicated you have not been looking into the economic measures from the point of view that would be the ultimate intentions. So I got your answer on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at the economic measures from the point of view of analysing the economic environment for the war economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. So if the intensions or part of the intentions were to establish some form of separate political entity in the territory of Herceg-Bosna, right, wouldn't it be necessary to pass laws, enactments on issues, such as finance, tax, customs, all of the things that you've looked at?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For region-wide authorities to undertake economic-wide measures which of course were needed because the situation in local communities were of a different situation, undertaking those measures was necessary. But that does not mean, right, that quote, that once they've done that, what would be the next step. What I would like of course to say in this respect is the following: I have seen and I was surprised of seeing the decree on the district which was for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm going to respectfully cut you off there. I think you've given a sufficient answer unless the Judges would like for you to continue, and we'll be talking about the districts later in my cross-examination. Isn't it possible that all of the legislation you looked at which you concluded was necessary to fill in the void, if you will, caused by the war in the situation, isn't it possible that such legislation is equally necessary to the establishment, the political establishment or the establishment of a separate political entity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because to establish a separate political entity within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right, the way it has been undertaken, the way I see those measures, these were the measures that were undertaken in the period of war and the imminent threat of war. I have not seen these measures that would be based on, I don't know, Republic of Croatia constitution or federal constitution, I have not seen those measures. I have seen those measures based upon the need to ensure the survival of the population on the territory in the same manner as I have seen those measures undertaken in the local communities of the Bosniaks majority where they have undertaken similar measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you rule out the possibility that the legislation of Herceg-Bosna could equally be intended to provide the legal framework for the establishment of a separate political entity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is a separate political entity within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would depend on what would be the constitutional structure of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about an entity such as is envisioned by the gentleman who wrote this -- the joint conclusions, for example, that we looked at. In order to establish that state that would be linked according to that to Croatia, it would be necessary to establish some laws if there's going to be a break; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which gentleman in which statement? Because you mentioned a couple of them, so I would just want to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This was the Exhibit P 00070. These are the joint --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If we are going to have a policy which will realise a common Croatian state, right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Proclamation of a Croatian banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it necessary to have legislation that would apply in such an area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way I understand the document P 00070 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I'm not asking if you understand the document, I'm just asking you as a general matter, isn't it true that legislation, some form of legislation would be necessary if we are going to create some new sort of political entity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this, one would first need an agreement within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that would be composed out of three areas that one would call whatever, banovinas or cantons or whatever, but that has not been agreed by that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did understand that all that was done still within the republic of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution where the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution had requested from the socio-economic communities Republic, like Opstinas, to undertake measures necessary to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's take the example of Slovenia, which you know very well, Slovenia declared its independence. It fought a war, a short war fortunately, and achieved its dependence, it achieved international recognition, and as part of that process it was obviously necessary for Slovenia to enact legislation in all of the economic spheres that you've described, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slovenia was, first of all, within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia not agreeing to the unitary state model in Yugoslavia, that's why Slovenia undertook measures to become independent state. Bosnia-Herzegovina was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not asking you to contrast the reasons why Slovenia sought independence. I'm asking you, isn't it true that Slovenia had to enact legislation on all of these financial customs, banking, all the rest, as part of its independence from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the same manner I was expecting the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would undertake such measures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The counsel and the witness are kindly asked to make pauses between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... respective independence are actually quite similar to the many measures taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, Mr. Stringer. I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer, to interrupt you, but the interpreters ask you but you didn't hear, that you have to slow down again and again and to pause between questions and answers. Please do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why don't you take Exhibit P 10767 which is in binder number 2. This is an article that you wrote in April of 1993 about Slovenian independence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The last document. Do you recognise this article?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote this article jointly with Mr. Kraft and Mr. Vodopivec.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to page 12, English version. This is section number 2, first economic experiences of independent Slovenia, and then specifically 2.1, gaining economic control. This is what you write: "To assert its economic self-determination, independent Slovenia needed to gain control of fiscal and monetary policy. Fiscal control proved easier because like other regions in former Yugoslavia, the fiscal system and policy had been for the most part under the control of the Slovenian authorities since the constitutional reform of 1974. To gain full control Slovenia simply stopped paying taxes to the federal government and took over customs." Mr. Cvikl, this is essentially the point I've been trying to make. As part of its independence, Slovenia was necessarily required to take measures, economic measures in order to gain control of its country, and would you agree with me that would require it to enact legislation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I said and that's exactly what I expected from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to undertake, to stop paying taxes to the federal government and took over customs, plus introduce currency on the day it declared independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. And in fact what we see in Herceg-Bosna is just that very thing. Except for the introduction of a new currency, they stopped paying tax, they took over customs, and they were enacting legislation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. First of all, they have not stopped paying taxes. They introduced new taxes because they were authorised to do that by the decree with the power of the law on the financing of the socio-economic needs. Second, they have undertaken the customs controls and the checking control points at the border because Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have not undertaken that. And they have not introduced new currency, but they have allowed a parallel currency to be in place like in other local communities all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. So the measures which they have undertaken are not the same as the measure which were undertaken in Slovenia. There is a quite important difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that if I were to put it to you that someone looking in all the activities and the legislation of Herceg-Bosna might conclude that this territory actually had its own intentions, independence or separateness, would you disagree with me? You reject that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the following reason: They were authorised by the decree issued by the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina to undertake measures, and they've done that because the central government authorities have not provided sources of funds for the functions of the local communities. They have undertaken establishing the customs points because Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina have not done that. And on the monetary, on the banking system, they have not established the banking system by themselves. The bank which operated down there got a licence from national bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they were undertaking economic measures on the economic territory which was freed and in order to reconnect local communities, and they have done the same measures which were done in the absence of the measures not being undertaken by the republican authorities by local communities all over Bosnia-Herzegovina especially in the Bosniak's controlled areas. And I don't know what was happening in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So then if I understand correctly what you are saying, then the political leadership of Herceg-Bosna, based on your review, had in your view no intentions in respect of independence or separateness in a political sense from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not asked to review that. I was asked to look into the economic measures, to analyse economic measures, interview what was happening in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the war situation, and I have seen lack of measures not being undertaken by the central government authorities, and I've seen that then there were measures in the first phase undertaken by the local communities all over the place. And later on for, in my view economic reasons, measures to ensure at the wider region support to the state and social services for the benefits of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 31 of this exhibit, your article on Slovenian independence. Halfway down the page you write: "Slovenia's experience suggests that cessation from a larger entity that is wrecked by political instability may have economic benefits. If local political autonomy provides the opportunity to introduce a new currency and achieve macroeconomic stabilization, separation can become economically attractive. However, this can only work if the local political constellation is not controlled by distributive coalitions bent on preserving the old redistributive system and is not hampered by major political divisions that paralyze decision-making. In short, cessation can be beneficial if the new state is more homogenous in its composition and coherent in its functioning than the old state was." Now, did you consider the extent to which Herceg-Bosna became or was ethnically homogenous in your assessment of its success or of its ability to implement economic measures that you've cited.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here I would like first to explain that this is the World Bank study. This is economic study. And when we talk about the homogenicity, here we think about the how economic system is homogenous, and here down in the next light I am of course mentioning the Czech-Slovak break-up.
