This was a study that was -- we were asked to write, Okay, what are the benefits, what are the costs if a bigger country, former Soviet Union, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, collapsed, and I have explained that already yesterday. If as a result of independence Slovenia or Czech Republic would be quicker in its place to undertake reforms, while reforms were before in old Yugoslavia politically blocked as I'm explaining in this article, right, this can only work if the political -- is not controlled by distributive coalitions, these are the distributive coalitions that were -- wanted to have a unitarian state within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia where there would be redistribution. Then only in these circumstances you have more economically homogenous country and you have coherent in its functioning, and the coherence in its functioning meaning that you have a more appropriate macroeconomic policies. And that's why I correctly mention about it inflation was dropping and not as it was in some other states. So it has nothing to do with the national homogeneity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nothing to do with ethnic homogeneity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this is not a study for, you know, general political science, this is a study of the World Bank on does it make sense for the World Bank to support, this is a very early study and it was a study which was also --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect I think --

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You've answer the question which was about the reference to homogeneity. I think that we can move on unless the Trial Chamber wants to hear more about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I take it the implication then is withdrawn by the Prosecution. The implication in the questioning that is, or maybe I'm just being paranoid at this stage of the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The question has been asked and it's been answered, I'm ready to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to return to document P 00302 which is the declaration of the decision on the establishment of the Croatian community that is in binder number 1. I have -- this document is important for the Trial Chamber. I would even go so far as to say it's fundamental because this document was taken the 18th of November 1991. 18th of November 1991 is the date according to the Prosecution of the date of the joint criminal enterprise, so it's an absolutely crucial document. You are not a lawyer, as you pointed out to us, and we've all taken due note of that. Notwithstanding that, I have a general question first of all, an economic question. On the general question, regarding the reason for the creation of this community. In paragraph 3 they explain why an application of the constitution and of the principles of the modern world with, of course, inalienable indivisible rights, non-transferrable, inexhaustible rights to self-determination and sovereignty including the right to association. Now, what I'd like to know is the right to association, which is a legal concept but which is known by all citizens, and in the former Yugoslavia, were persons private individuals or public entities, were they entitled to association? Was this a right that was recognised in former Yugoslavia? If the question is too legal, please say so and you can't answer, but if you do know, please answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the right to association was actually in the old Yugoslav self-management system one of the rights which was actually quite well practiced. It is the right to even the basic enterprise was called associated organisation of labour, and those associated organisation of labour then were merged into a bigger company. So if you ask me, the so-called right on association was actually one of the elements why we have this Self-Management Interest Communities where on one side you associated the buyers and on the other side providers of the services. So the right to association was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So on this model, it would appear that the communities set out in Article 2 that the local communities will associate. So that answers part of my question. But look at Article 1, please, and just explain it to us slowly in economic terms. When you read this article in economic terms, what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the way I read this first article reason, as an economist, and that is of course it goes back to the story of the collapse of Yugoslavia. We all knew that it would be a relatively easy to achieve independence as republics for Slovenia, for Croatia, even for Macedonia, also as you know very well later for the republic of Montenegro. But as the third paragraph of that first article talks about the -- these three constitute peoples in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was perceived in old Yugoslavia as mini Yugoslavia, as mini Yugoslavia. There were three constitute peoples. It of course, one would assume if one follows what was happening in Slovenia, in Macedonia, in Montenegro, in Croatia, how to solve what was then solved with the Dayton agreement, is a kind of a respecting these, you know, constituent right of the three constituent peoples, with the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with these ten Cantons, and Republika Srpska. And in that context, I read this decision on establishment of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna for the economic point of view as a way how one, you know, somehow economically link these local municipalities and tried to, of course, present that for them the unitary state model is not acceptable. So somehow the -- if there would be a peaceful solution and a respectful or economically viable peaceful solution would be some kind of the, you know, quote within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina borders, some kind of three distinct economic areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise, but there seems to be a mistake in the transcript and I think it's very important for understanding what Mr. Cvikl just told us, and it's in line -- or rather page 92, line 2, and what was recorded was the following: [In English] [Microphone not activated] ... was perceived in old Yugoslavia as there were three constituent peoples." The witness in fact said that in the former Yugoslavia Bosnia-Herzegovina was considered Yugoslavia in miniature. A small Yugoslavia. And then a large Yugoslavia on unitary basis could not survive, et cetera. So that is the substance of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a nutshell regarding this article which is a very basic article, economically speaking, I'm not talking about politics or culture, you say that economically speaking this article means that the municipalities mentioned in Article 2 wanted to create an economic link among themselves, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm saying that the local communities which are mentioned in Article 2 wanted in the circumstances were they were not accepting the unitary state model in Bosnia-Herzegovina, assure economic interconnection with them, and then utilized that if there would be a serious discussion, this is the time, understand the time of the independence of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina what shall be a constitution of Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina look like. And if that constitution should follow what was actually happening with the collapse of Yugoslavia because nobody in Yugoslavia wanted to have a unitarian state, there shall be some kind of smaller units within this Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's why I have said what was then resulted at the end in during the Dayton agreement is some kind of such a resolution. Two entities and one entity the Federation with ten Cantons. But we are not yet at that stage. At that stage we had only 109, 108 local communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But of course, the way the Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina writes and all these things were undertaken, that was still part of the Federation of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, going back to your earlier question, it may be of some assistance if you were to look at 1D 02994 which is the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina article -- starting with Article 274 where it talks about cooperation in association by municipalities. I draw that to your attention in light of the question that you did pose earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now speaking to the expert in economics. I understood what you said, you said that since there was some kind of fear to which the unitary model, these communities wanted to create a link among themselves. That is understandable. But is this economic approach not in contradiction to the European models here that you know very well, which is basically the integration of economies in the European Union? You then have a unique or only one economy into which all the countries will integrate, Belgium or Slovenia. So isn't this text contradictory to the overall project of European integration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, because one should not look to European Union as the United States of Europe of 27 countries now, but one should look to the European Union as the federation of regions. And when you look into particular European Union state, for example Slovakia. Economically speaking what is integrated in European Union is not Slovakia itself but actually four regions of Slovakia, and the integration and the cohesion which we try to achieve within the European Union is not just the cohesion among the 27 states, but is the cohesion among the level of the development of the regions in a particular country, like, for example, Slovakia. In Belgium we see there are actually also three regions, Netherlands same, et cetera. So the European Union for freedoms of movements, movements of goods, people, et cetera, they are an instrument, how we assure cohesion, but that is not a melting pot of United States of Europe. This is European Union of 27 countries trying to achieve cohesion on a much lower level, so-called regions. And what I would be expecting in Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina would be at least couple of regions where the fact that there are three constituent people, there would be appropriate cohesion of policies in these regions so that all three regions or four or five or six would have meaningful equal level of development. If you look to the neighbouring Republic of Croatia, there are zupanjas [phoen], there are seven regions, I believe seven, something like that, where there is, you know, interconnections among the local municipalities. So I do not see any of this what was happening as opposed to the modern European Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is extremely clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cvikl, I'm going to take you back to something that you said a few minutes ago, try to wrap this up. If I understand correctly, your review of the decree establishing Herceg-Bosna from an economic point of view would imply some kind of distinct economic area. I'll read the words back to you. You were talking -- you said -- you made reference to a respectful, viable, peaceful solution would be some kind of a "within the border some kind of three distinct economic areas." That's what you just said. So I guess at a minimum from an economic point of view, is it your testimony that this document implies the establishment of a distinct economic area within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This document implies there will be a discussion on how Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution will be further developed, and clearly these 18 or however many local communities would have a serious voice in this discussion. And I would even go further, the Dayton constitution has taken this stance that there is at least two distinctive economic areas being the fact that there are two economic entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, that last point you made is an interesting one in terms of who has the serious voice in the discussion because you were talking earlier about all of the 30 municipalities that joined the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now, have you considered or do you know the legal process whereby those municipalities joined Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I understood that in the fall of 1991 there were elections which means that -- and then under these elections there were elections in free elections political leaders of particular local municipalities and I believe that these were legal representative of people elected at free elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So your assumption is that each of these municipalities, the lawfully elected leaders of the municipalities each on behalf of their municipalities joined Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Or do you know? Are you just assuming that that is what took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- I don't know what happened and how did decision came to -- you know, how did this meeting took place, et cetera. I only know that there were elections that people who represent the local communities were elected at free elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, are you aware, sir, that in September of 1992 the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina annulled the decree on the establishment of Herceg-Bosna and also annulled a number of other fundamental pieces of legislation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about it, but I only know that somewhere in June or July of -- somewhat before that, the state of war was declared in -- on the territory of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I'm not aware of that, and I would be surprised if they had done that because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Sorry, I'm not asking you to speculate about whether you are surprised as what the constitutional court did. I'm simply asking you as a follow-up to other questions, did you know. Your answer is no, you did not know about this decision. My next question, then, is, if you had known about this decision, would it affect your conclusions about the activities and the intentions of Herceg-Bosna throughout 1992 and 1993 after this decision was issued?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I would expect that the constitutional court to annul at the same time the decision of the presidency of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware that in January of 1994, the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina annulled the decision on the proclamation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and if not, would that affect your opinion in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like, of course, to read the explanation of that very decision by the constitutional court before I answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The question was, are you aware of it? I can take you to it. It's in the binder P 08060.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Binder 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Binder number 1. 8060. 8060.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, Your Honour, before we have the answer. I assume Mr. Stringer is going to lay a foundation to the effect that the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina was then, as it was during the previous decision, duly constituted and was legally functioning, as opposed to it being a rump, a rump constitutional court representing only one of the people's in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, speeches like that which feed and suggest answers to witnesses are highly improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They don't feed or suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's highly improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with whether he understands or knows it. I -- he is providing a particular decision, and I am saying at some point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We need a foundation as to whether this decision was lawful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you are an excellent lawyer, you know better than anyone that this is a question that has been dealt with in this courtroom numberless times so the trial judges are perfectly aware of that decision and everything underlying it. We know that. We know that. I could speak about it for hours. So we are perfectly in the know of things. Now, the interesting part is the witness's answer to the Prosecutor's question. That's the thing that is of interest to us now. I know that he is not a lawyer, but it could shed some light. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I also object on a different basis. The point is that the Prosecutor is now asking the witness about what would be the situation if he would have known that there was a constitutional court decision which nullified the existence of Herceg-Bosna, HZ HB. This is entirely out of scope of this report. And by the way, Your Honour, my dear colleague on the Prosecution desk has made exactly the same objection to my cross-examination even though I asked the witness something which he testified while here in the court. But the Prosecution then objected on the basis that this specific subject matter was not raised by the expert report. So I'm repeating that objection. It is not in the expert report. This is simply an exercise what would have been if you would have known this. This is speculative. This is no worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, in his report, in the examination-in-chief, the expert explains why the local communities wanted to set up links among themselves for various reasons. We know that. As it were, he thinks that this was imposed by the situation. And now the Prosecutor, and that is his basic right, he wants to submit a document to the expert, a document that shows that the judges of a constitutional court came to the opposite decision. The witness might say well, the judges were right or they were wrong. Let's wait and see. Mr. Stringer, once we were speaking, the witness must have read the decision, so please put your question again and we'll see what his answer will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll just break it down into a couple of short questions, maybe we can get short answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you provided this decision or a copy of it as part of your review and analysis, preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Secondly, were you otherwise aware of this document based on your having been working in and around the region of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not looking to the decision of the constitutional courts of Bosnia-Herzegovina of January 20th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. And then the last question is, now that you've seen the decision and you are aware of it and you've had a chance to read it, would it affect the conclusions and opinions, findings that you've made in your report on the intentions and the efforts of the HVO, the authorities of, in this case, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm an economist so I'm reading this decision of the constitution court as an economist and there is a statement that I disagree with. The statement goes something like this, with this decision -- I will do it in English though, just a second. The decision, it says that -- I will read the Bosnian Croatian words so I will ask them to be translated into English. The constitutional court says: [Interpretation] "In this manner, in an unconstitutional manner --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, the interpreters will want assistance. This is a one-page document. Could you give precisely the location where the interpreters find it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm reading the document provided by Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where on the page can the interpreters go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is page 6 -- number 6, page 85 of the Bosnian version, and that is the third paragraph -- first paragraph on the right-hand side. And it says: [Interpretation] "Thereby, in an unconstitutional manner, an effort is made to disrupt the constitutionally enshrined integrity of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the equal status of its citizens ," and so on and so forth. The measures undertaken by the region-wide authorities, I have not seen that those measures would exclude or take out of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina a particular area of the Croatian community or of the later Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And that's why the -- my analysis on the economic measures undertaken within the economic environment in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina if I would see that before would not be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Isn't it possible that the scope of the analysis conducted by the constitutional court was broader than just the economic sphere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would respond differently. I would expect that by this what you have just said the Dayton constitution would be also defined by the constitutional court as unlawful, because the constitutional Dayton talks about two entities and these two entities would be unlawful according to the then Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution. So it's a kind of a chicken and egg, you know. Here we are talking about what the constitutional court agreed on January 1994, where on February 1994, I believe there was the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina politically established. So as an economist, I'm reading this decision claiming that with this decision the territory had been broken up. I have not seen that. I have not seen on the administrative borders, or what was before the war, borders of Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I have seen those borders being established. There would be borders established between the border of local municipality of Jablanica, and local municipality of Hadzici which means within the borders, then I would take this for granted, but it was not. The customs points and the checking points were established in the outside borders of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So for all economic reasoning whatever was happening within the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was happening within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina economically and also, I believe, politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in your view, sir, the decision of the constitutional court of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina here is an incorrect decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, and I'm not judging what the constitutional court is saying. You asked me whether my analysis would be different, my analysis would not be different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MILAN CVIKL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I looked into the economical part of it and I would also assume that that was actually the reasoning why the World Bank team when assisting to the economist rewriting Dayton constitution actually supporting the Federation and Republika Srpska as economic entity to remain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you some questions now about the part of your report, and I suppose it relates to phase 1 in that it relates primarily to the municipalities. In your report you refer to the constitutional role, the enhanced role of the municipality within Bosnia-Herzegovina, and actually in the former Yugoslavia in time of war. And if you could take Exhibit 1D 02994, which is in binder 3. You referred to this, this is the constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you move on to that document, I'd like to return to the decision of the constitutional court. You are not a lawyer, but you do have some knowledge. You know that back then -- or did you know that there were discussions on a peace conference in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- we were aware of different versions of these discussions in 1993, 1994 period because we in the World Bank were waiting what would be the outcome of these different plans that were at the time up and running.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason why I'm asking you this is that in the last paragraph of the decision because the judges of that court are judges after all, and sometimes judges can come up with excellent decisions, and they say this: The decision to proclaim the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna should not be founded on the document of the agreement of the Federation of the Republic of Bosnia which is being discussed at the peace conference in Geneva, because the document was not adopted by the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the only competent body to change the constitution. In saying so, did the constitutional judges not open a door by saying that we rule that it is not constitutional, but there are talks in Geneva and this solution goes through Geneva, goes through the assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that can change the constitution. So was this a constitutional decision that was sort of without any hope, or was a door left open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't comment on that, but clearly what the judges are here saying from what I understand at that time, of course, is that of course the parliament of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not meet. So there was the presidency, if any one would want to go this way, then the presidency could eventually make such a decision. What was then happening in the Geneva, and that is of course it's quite different. Federation of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was something that would be different than what later came in in the Dayton. So we were at that time in the World Bank waiting what would be the outcome, you know, because everybody wanted to have peace and wanted to have going back to trying to solve economic problems in whatever will be the constitutional environment. And I'm only saying that the ultimate constitutional environment which resulted out of Dayton agreement would be also taking and reading these decisions by the judges declared as unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We have five minutes left, Mr. Stringer, sorry for returning to the document but we talk a lot about this document. And you produced it, anyway. One more reason to speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm the guilty party. Mr. President, I'm just about to enter into a different topic and I would respectfully suggest it's a good time to break, and could I add if I could have 30 seconds to address the Trial Chamber about another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Yes, you can do that. In terms of time, I'm a little worried. You have used 1 hour and 38 minutes. You have 2 hours and 22 minutes left. So I'll try not to ask questions tomorrow and we'll try to let you use that time you have so that the witness can leave this week. Can you speak about that subject with the witness in the courtroom or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Yes, it's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's related actually. My first comment was to express some concern about the timing. I know that Mr. Cvikl wants to leave tomorrow or to complete his testimony tomorrow and not to come back. And as you've pointed out, I'm mildly getting concerned about that. I think based on where I am in my outline I will require the full four hours. In addition, Mr. President, we did want to at some point, and I don't know whether it will be time tomorrow, just to mention the issue of scheduling in respect to the following witness because based upon the additional amounts of time that are -- have been sought by other Defence teams in respect of the first witness, the expert witness for the Stojic team, we think it appears quite likely that that witness could go well into a second week. We also understand that the Stojic team will be making an opening statement of some sort which would obviously require time, and our only point right now, Mr. President, is to raise this, and perhaps there's more time for us all to reflect on it, but certainly I think we all need to consider the extent to which the trial calendar is going to be changed based upon the witness next week and the opening statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you need four hours for this witness. You have used 1 hour and 30 minutes, so you have 2 hours and 22 minutes left. So in theory, we should have four hours tomorrow so that should be fine, enough time for you to wrap it up, no problem, I think. Now, as for next week from memory because I don't have the papers in front of me, I think that the Stojic Defence will require four hours for examination-in-chief, the others will have three hours. So we have one half-hours and one half-hours altogether is three hours. As to the Prosecution, as far as I know they will have four hours. We might not be able to finish the testimony in one week so Ms. Nozica's witness will have to continue the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And maybe we should add that we have been seized of a request for additional time and that has not yet been set or decided upon by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, indeed, there's that additional problem. But what I was saying that was before the filing of the request for review by the Petkovic Defence, so it could well be that that witness, the first for Ms. Nozica, will have to continue at least until Tuesday or -- Monday or Tuesday of the following week.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If I could just make one comment, Mr. President. It's based upon the guide-lines. The supplemental -- any supplemental time that goes beyond cross-examination of other teams, I think, would then result in greater time being available to the Prosecution for cross-examination, and so it may be that the Prosecution will be entitled to or will require more than four hours. Obviously I don't know if that will happen, but it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the more reason for you to state your position by Friday. That is the reason why I asked for it. Yes, Witness, well you are the main person concerned here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just would like to ask the Court if it's possible in order to save on time tomorrow whether I can read these documents overnight because I can't read them here. I just want to save sometime otherwise tomorrow I would have to be familiarise myself with the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You like to take the Prosecution documents with you? Well, we have precedents and there was no problem from the Trial Chamber's point of view. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: There have been rare occasions, Mr. President however, if I can refer to the rules of the game invoked earlier by Judge Trechsel, we would be opposed to the witness taking the documents with him. I think that cross-examination from our view requires that he be looking at the documents fresh as they are put in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, you know in these proceedings, typically Anglo-Saxon proceedings, and you know them because you live in the United States, it's always the effect of surprise. The one cross-examining would like to surprise or take the witness by surprise. That's part of the tactics. And so that is why there's some reluctance on the part of the Prosecutor, can you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just was taking into account that they have a -- they are short on time and there's lot of documents, I would of course as they would be shown to me I would have to look at them, that will go against the time that the Prosecution has for questions, that's why I asked. If they oppose, I will read something else in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the Prosecutor had agreed, it would have been no problem, but he doesn't agree so you can't take the documents with you anyway. You are so competent that even if you see a document you will be able to react straightaway so you should not be prejudiced. Yes, Ms. Nozica, did you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I merely wanted to say quite briefly that Mr. Stojic's Defence will not be presenting an opening statement, that means that if we complete the testimony of this witness on Monday we will be able to call the expert witness of the Defence. We understood the position of the Trial Chamber regarding additional time. We will be filing a written submission, but for the transcript, for the record, I would like to say that we would like to express our concern that we would be in a position to seek supplemental time for redirect because this is the way we planned our time in accordance with the decision of the Chamber regarding the time allotted to the Defence -- to the other Defences and the Prosecution for the cross-examination, that's what I'm talking about, because any increases of the time for the cross-examination would require an increase in the time for the redirect, and since we have already made our plan and since we have submitted it to the Chamber, leaving enough time for us that we consider we need, if any requests made by the other parties for an increase in the time allotted for the cross-examination, we would be submitting our own requests to that effect. I would just like to make that clear right at the outset to avoid any surprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, of course you are entitled to redirect, but that is time taken out of your overall time, but you might not need to use that time if you don't have redirect. I'm always surprised that a Defence team might think that there would be contradictions arising from other Defence teams. In theory it's possible, but it's rather rare. But admittedly if you want a time for redirect no problem, you'll have it. As part of the overall time allotted to you. He is your witness, so I suppose you sort of envisaged all the problems with you. He will be aware of things, and if he is not finished by next week he will come back. Sometimes you have witnesses that come to testify for two, three, if not four weeks. We know that. Sorry for the time -- for the extra time, but that had to be done. I wish you all a good evening. We shall reconvene tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of January 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.
